name: Riau-Lingga Sultanate
description: The Riau-Lingga Sultanate was an island realm in Maritime Southeast Asia established following the territorial division of the historic Johor Empire under the 1824 Anglo-Dutch Treaty. Governed from royal courts at Daik and administrative offices in Tanjungpinang, the sultanate commanded crucial maritime trade routes across the Riau and Lingga archipelagos. Its autonomy gradually eroded under expanding Dutch imperial oversight until colonial authorities formally dissolved the monarchy in 1911. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Daik; Common languages: Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Johor Sultanate; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Malacca
description: Malacca was a British crown holding on the south-western coast of the Malay Peninsula, administered temporarily as a distinct colonial possession following its transfer from Dutch rule under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824. Centred on the ancient port city beside the Malacca Strait, the settlement served as a strategic maritime station for British commercial shipping. This interim administration concluded in August 1826 when British authorities merged the port with Penang and Singapore into the Straits Settlements. \n\n Status: British colony; Capital: Malacca; Common languages: Classical Malay and English; Religion: Sunni Islam and Christianity; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Dutch Malacca; Succeeded by: Straits Settlements

name: Republic of Bolivia
description: The Republic of Bolivia was a sovereign South American state established in August 1825 following the liberation of Upper Peru from Spanish imperial dominion. Headquartered constitutionally at Sucre, the nation spanned the high Andean Altiplano, fertile valleys and eastern tropical lowlands. Bolivia maintained its republican governance through numerous territorial conflicts with neighbouring states and internal constitutional reforms until reconstituting itself as a plurinational republic in 2009. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Sucre; Official languages: Spanish, Quechua and Aymara; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Plurinational Legislative Assembly; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Real Audiencia of Charcas; Succeeded by: Plurinational State of Bolivia

name: Colony of Van Diemen's Land
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Colony of Van Diemen's Land was a British penal colony occupying the island of Tasmania south of the Australian mainland. Administered from Hobart after separating from New South Wales in December 1825, the settlement became notorious for its highly regimented secondary punishment stations at Macquarie Harbour and Port Arthur. Following the cessation of convict transportation and the granting of responsible self-government, the colony was renamed Tasmania in 1856 to shed its penal connotations. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Hobart; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Self-governing colony; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: Victorian era; Preceded by: Colony of New South Wales; Succeeded by: Colony of Tasmania

name: Emirate of Trarza
description: The Emirate of Trarza was a traditional nomadic confederation in south-western Mauritania that operated as a French protectorate following the conclusion of the Franco-Trarzan War. Led by Hassaniya-speaking Arab warrior clans, the emirate dominated the lucrative gum arabic trade along the northern banks of the lower Senegal River. Internal dynastic rivalries and encroaching European military posts gradually weakened native authority until French colonial forces formally annexed the territory into French West Africa in 1903. \n\n Status: French protectorate; Administrative seat: Mederdra; Common languages: Hassaniya Arabic, Zenaga and Wolof; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Gaza Empire
label: polities of the swahili coast
description: The Gaza Empire was a formidable militarised realm in south-eastern Africa founded by the Nguni leader Soshangane during the upheavals of the Mfecane migrations. Centred around royal residences at Manjacaze, the empire stretched across southern Mozambique between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, subjugating surrounding Tsonga and Shona communities. Gaza retained formidable military prowess and political independence until Portuguese imperial forces defeated its final ruler, Ngungunhane, in December 1895. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Manjacaze; Common languages: Nguni and Tsonga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1824; Disestablished: 28 December 1895

name: Kutlehar State
label: indian princely states
description: Kutlehar State was a small Hindu princely principality in the Punjab Hills region of northern India, ruled by an ancient Rajput lineage. Based at the fortified stronghold of Kot Kutlehar, the state maintained local autonomy under British paramountcy following the Anglo-Sikh Wars and the pacification of the Kangra hills. Its rulers retained their ancestral estate and ceremonial privileges through the twilight of the British Raj until integrating into independent India. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Kot Kutlehar; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Autocracy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Lapai Emirate
label: fula jihads polities
description: The Lapai Emirate was a traditional Muslim principality established near the Gurara River in central Nigeria as an outcome of the nineteenth-century Fulani jihad. Carved out from the frontiers of Zaria and Agaie, the state was ruled by Nupe and Fulani commanders who held nominal allegiance to the Gwandu emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate. Lapai maintained commercial networks and local self-rule until British forces under the Royal Niger Company subdued the emirate in June 1898. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Administrative seat: Lapai; Common languages: Nupe and Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1825; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Thani Domain
description: The Thani Domain was an emerging coastal sheikhdom on the eastern shores of the Arabian Peninsula, established under the leadership of Sheikh Mohammed bin Thani. Based around the port settlement of Al Bidda, the domain derived its wealth and influence from pearling fleets and regional maritime commerce across the Persian Gulf. After navigating persistent conflicts with neighbouring Bahrain and Abu Dhabi, the domain secured separate recognition from Great Britain in 1868, establishing the modern foundation of Qatar. \n\n Status: Sovereign sheikhdom; Capital: Al Bidda; Common languages: Gulf Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sheikhdom; Ruling dynasty: House of Thani; Ruler title: Sheikh; Historical era: Modern era; Succeeded by: State of Qatar

name: Straits Settlements
description: The Straits Settlements formed a vital British colonial jurisdiction in Southeast Asia, originally consolidated in August 1826 by uniting Penang, Malacca and Singapore under East India Company administration. Designated a British crown colony in 1867 with Singapore as its primary administrative capital, the dependency governed critical chokepoints along the Malacca Strait. The territories flourished as bustling entrepôts for international trade and immigration until imperial Japanese forces invaded and occupied the settlements in February 1942. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Singapore; Common languages: English, Malay, Chinese and Tamil; Religion: Islam, Buddhism and Christianity; Government: Crown colony administration; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: British Empire; Preceded by: Dutch Malacca; Succeeded by: Colony of Singapore

name: Sonepur State
label: indian princely states
description: Sonepur State was a princely principality in western Odisha along the banks of the Mahanadi and Tel rivers, governed by rulers of the Chauhan Rajput dynasty. Headquartered at the historic town of Sonepur, the state was administered successively under the Central India Agency and the Eastern States Agency of British India. Its rulers exercised judicial and civil authority over agrarian and forested tracts until formally acceding to the Indian Union in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Sonepur; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1650; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Adam Kok's Land
label: boer states
description: Adam Kok's Land was an autonomous Griqua republic situated north of the Orange River in the southern interior of southern Africa. Centred at the settlement of Philippolis, the polity was led by Kaptyn Adam Kok and a council of Dutch-speaking pastoralists of mixed ancestry who had migrated inland from the Cape Colony. Facing relentless land encroachment from advancing Boer pastoralists and British boundary adjustments, the community maintained independence until abandoning the region in 1861 to trek eastwards toward Griqualand East. \n\n Status: Autonomous republic; Capital: Philippolis; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Semi-republican captaincy; Ruler title: Kaptyn; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1827; Succeeded by: Orange Free State

name: Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
label: german confederation
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha was a sovereign Ernestine principality in central Germany created through dynastic reallocation among the Wettin ducal lines following the extinction of Saxe-Gotha-Altenburg. Operating under a personal union with dual capitals at Coburg and Gotha, the state wielded prominent diplomatic influence across nineteenth-century European royal houses. It maintained full sovereignty as a member state of the German Confederation until joining the unified German Empire in January 1871. \n\n Status: Sovereign duchy; Capital: Coburg and Gotha; Official languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: German Confederation; Succeeded by: German Empire

name: Jambughoda State
label: indian princely states
description: Jambughoda State was a small princely estate located in eastern Gujarat, ruled by a dynasty of Parmar Rajputs and earlier known as Narukot. Administered under the Baroda Agency of the Bombay Presidency, the principality covered hilly forested terrain predominantly populated by Naikda and Koli communities. British political agents supervised the territory during extended periods of direct management before its hereditary thakurs oversaw its eventual accession to India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jambughoda; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruler title: Thakur; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Baroda Agency; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Lunavada State
label: indian princely states
description: Lunavada State was a second-class princely state situated along the Mahi River in the Rewa Kantha region of Gujarat. Governed from the town of Lunavada by rulers of the Solanki Rajput dynasty, the polity maintained domestic autonomy under subsidiary treaties negotiated with the British East India Company. The state retained its traditional governance and nine-gun salute status through the British Raj until merging into the Indian Union in June 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Lunavada; Common languages: Gujarati and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Maharana; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1434; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Kingdom of Vientiane and Kingdom of Champasak (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Vientiane and Kingdom of Champasak Military Occupation encompassed central Siamese borderlands temporarily overrun by allied Lao royal forces during the Anouvong Rebellion in early 1827. Spearheaded by King Anouvong of Vientiane and his son Chao Yo of Champasak, the offensive seized control across the Khorat Plateau toward Saraburi without establishing a permanent civil capital. Siamese counter-offensives rapidly reversed these advances by mid-1827, precipitating the comprehensive defeat and sack of Vientiane. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Lao and Siamese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military occupation; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1 February 1827; Disestablished: 1 July 1827

name: Bonin Islands
description: The Bonin Islands comprised an isolated subtropical volcanic archipelago in the north-western Pacific Ocean claimed as a British colonial dependency by Captain Frederick William Beechey of HMS Blossom in June 1827. Headquartered at the natural harbour of Port Lloyd on Chichijima, the islands provided a strategic waystation and victualling post for Pacific whalers and merchant vessels. British claims lapsed as multiracial settlers arrived from Hawaii and North America, ultimately leading to Japan formally asserting sovereign control over the archipelago in the Meiji era. \n\n Status: British colonial claim; Administrative seat: Chichijima; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Naval colonial dependency; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 14 June 1827; Succeeded by: Meiji Japan

name: Republic of Madawaska
description: The Republic of Madawaska was an ephemeral, unrecognised frontier republic declared on 4 July 1827 by American settler John Baker in the upper Saint John River valley. Established across disputed borderlands between Maine, Lower Canada and New Brunswick, the putative state sought to challenge British jurisdiction and encourage American annexation. British colonial authorities from New Brunswick promptly suppressed the rebellion in September 1827, arresting Baker and restoring imperial administrative control over the settlement. \n\n Status: Unrecognised republic; Capital: Madawaska; Common languages: English and French; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional republic; Ruler title: General; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 4 July 1827; Disestablished: 25 September 1827

name: Erivan Khanate
description: The Erivan Khanate was a transitional Caucasian administrative principality centred at Yerevan that fell under Russian imperial vassalage in October 1827 during the closing stages of the Russo-Persian War. Russian military authorities occupied the fortress city and supervised local Muslim and Armenian notables following the retreat of Qajar forces. This brief interim status concluded in February 1828 with the Treaty of Turkmenchay, which formally ceded the khanate to the Russian Empire and led to the creation of the Armenian Oblast. \n\n Status: Imperial vassal; Capital: Yerevan; Common languages: Persian, Armenian and Azerbaijani; Religion: Shia Islam and Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Military vassal administration; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Qajar Iran; Succeeded by: Armenian Oblast

name: Allied Protector Army of the Law
description: The Allied Protector Army of the Law was a liberal revolutionary military organisation formed across Central America under the command of General Francisco Morazán during the First Central American Civil War. Operating as an itinerant mobile force without a fixed civil capital, the movement arose to oppose the centralist and conservative policies of Federal President Manuel José Arce. After sweeping across Honduras and El Salvador, Morazán's army captured Guatemala City in April 1829, ending the civil war and restoring liberal governance to the Central American federation. \n\n Status: Revolutionary military government; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military command; Ruler title: General; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 11 November 1827; Disestablished: 12 April 1829

name: Ningi
description: Ningi was an independent non-Muslim and dissident chiefdom in northern Nigeria, established within rugged hill country north of Bauchi around 1828. Founded by refugees and dissenters led by Mallam Hamza who rejected the authority of the Sokoto Caliphate, the state maintained a formidable cavalry army to repel Fulani jihadist incursions. Governed from the fortified settlement of Ningi, the polity retained fierce territorial autonomy and conducted extensive raiding across neighbouring emirates until British forces pacified the region in 1900. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ningi; Common languages: Hausa and Ningi; Religion: Traditional African religion and Islam; Government: Traditional chiefdom; Ruler title: Mallam; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Disestablished: 1900

name: Port Clarence
description: Port Clarence was a British naval station and leased settlement established on the northern coast of Fernando Po in the Gulf of Guinea under agreement with Spain. Functioning from the harbour site that later became Malabo, the base served as a primary operational hub for the Royal Navy West Africa Squadron in suppressing the transatlantic slave trade and resettling liberated Africans. Great Britain administered the leased facility until 1844, when operational duties shifted elsewhere and Spanish imperial authorities resumed direct supervision of the island. \n\n Status: Leased naval station; Administrative seat: Malabo; Common languages: English, Spanish and Pichinglis; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Naval administration; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Disestablished: 1844

name: Somaliland Protectorate
description: The Somaliland Protectorate was a British dependency in the Horn of Africa situated along the southern shores of the Gulf of Aden. Initially established through maritime treaties with local Somali clan leaders and administered successively from coastal Berbera and inland Hargeisa, the territory safeguarded imperial maritime trade routes linking the Suez Canal to British India. Although briefly overrun by Italian forces during the Second World War in 1940, British control was restored in 1941, persisting until the territory gained full independence in June 1960. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Hargeisa; Common languages: Somali, Arabic and English; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Modern era; Succeeded by: State of Somaliland

name: Republic of Peru (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of Peru Military Occupation designated external territories held under martial administration by the Peruvian armed forces during regional conflicts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Initiated during General Agustín Gamarra's expedition into Bolivia in 1828 and the subsequent naval occupation of Guayaquil, the operational command operated without a permanent territorial capital. Peruvian military authorities oversaw garrisons and provisional civil affairs until diplomatic treaties restored local governance or negotiated boundary settlements. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military occupation; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1 May 1828

name: Oriental Republic of Uruguay
description: The Oriental Republic of Uruguay was established in August 1828 as an independent buffer state along the northern shore of the Río de la Plata following the Treaty of Montevideo. Headquartered in Montevideo, the republic emerged from bitter territorial contention between the United Provinces of the River Plate and the Empire of Brazil over the former Cisplatine province. Despite protracted civil conflicts between Colorados and Blancos during the nineteenth century, Uruguay developed a robust constitutional democracy and commercial economy oriented toward maritime trade. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Montevideo; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: General Assembly; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 27 August 1828; Preceded by: Cisplatina Province

name: Caucasian Imamate
description: The Caucasian Imamate was a theocratic Islamic state established across the mountainous highlands of Dagestan and Chechnya to coordinate native resistance against the expansion of the Russian Empire. Governed by a succession of charismatic religious leaders, most famously Imam Shamil from his fortified mountain capital at Vedeno, the state enforced strict sharia law and built a disciplined military confederation. Decades of asymmetric warfare during the Caucasian War concluded in 1859 when Russian forces captured Shamil, bringing the imamate to an end. \n\n Status: Sovereign imamate; Capital: Vedeno; Common languages: Arabic, Avar, Chechen and Kumyk; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic theocracy; Ruler title: Imam; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Disestablished: 1859; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Emirate of Abuja
label: fula jihads polities
description: The Emirate of Abuja was a traditional Hausa kingdom founded in central Nigeria by the deposed Habe ruling dynasty of Zazzau following their expulsion from Zaria by Fulani jihadists. Establishing their stronghold near Zuma Rock at modern-day Suleja, the emirs retained ancient Hausa royal customs, administrative rituals and military autonomy while repelling repeated Fulani invasions. The emirate retained full sovereignty and dominated regional trade routes until British colonial forces conquered the territory in 1903. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Administrative seat: Abuja; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam and traditional religions; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Disestablished: 1903; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kentucky in Africa
label: us colonies in liberia
description: Kentucky in Africa was an American settlement colony established along the banks of the Saint Paul River under the auspices of the Kentucky State Colonisation Society. Centred on the riverine settlement of Clay-Ashland, the colony was settled by emancipated slaves and freeborn African Americans transported from the state of Kentucky. The fledgling community built agricultural homesteads and churches while navigating complex relations with indigenous peoples before formally integrating into the Commonwealth of Liberia in the 1840s. \n\n Status: American colonisation colony; Capital: Clay-Ashland; Common languages: English; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Disestablished: 1843; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Liberia

name: Phulra State
description: Phulra State was a minor Muslim mountain principality situated in the rugged Tanawal region of the North-West Frontier along the upper Indus River. Ruled by hereditary khans of the Hindkowan Tanoli lineage from their seat at Phulra, the state originated as a semi-independent feudatory granted by the ruler of neighbouring Amb. The principality preserved internal autonomy and tribal self-governance across the nineteenth century before formalising its subordinate relationship as a princely state under the British Raj. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Phulra; Common languages: Hindko and Pashto; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1828; Preceded by: Amb State

name: Swan River Colony
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Swan River Colony was a British free settlement established in May 1829 along the Swan River on the south-western coast of New Holland. Founded by Lieutenant-Governor James Stirling with its administrative headquarters at Perth and its port at Fremantle, the enterprise was planned as an exclusively civilian agricultural colony without convict transportation. Severe environmental challenges and slow population growth led imperial authorities to reorganise the territory in February 1832 as the Colony of Western Australia. \n\n Status: British colony; Capital: Perth; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Crown colony; Ruler title: Lieutenant-Governor; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 2 May 1829; Disestablished: 6 February 1832; Succeeded by: Colony of Western Australia

name: Principality of Moldavia
description: The Principality of Moldavia was an autonomous Danubian principality that operated under an imperial Russian protectorate following the Treaty of Adrianople in September 1829. Governed from Iași under the constitutional provisions of the Regulamentul Organic, the state remained nominally tributary to the Ottoman Sublime Porte while Russian commissioners supervised political administration and judicial reforms. This period of dual influence fostered national awakening and institutional modernisation until the outbreak of the Crimean War terminated direct Russian administrative oversight in 1853. \n\n Status: Russian protectorate; Capital: Iași; Common languages: Romanian and Russian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Hospodar; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 14 September 1829; Disestablished: 1 June 1853

name: Principality of Wallachia
description: The Principality of Wallachia was an autonomous Romanian state located between the Southern Carpathians and the Danube that came under direct Russian imperial protection in September 1829. Administered from Bucharest according to the quasi-constitutional Regulamentul Organic, the principality experienced substantial administrative reorganisations and urban expansion while technically preserving Ottoman suzerainty. Russian diplomatic and military supervision persisted through repeated revolutionary upheavals until the outbreak of the Crimean War prompted Russian forces to withdraw in 1853. \n\n Status: Russian protectorate; Capital: Bucharest; Common languages: Romanian and Russian; Religion: Romanian Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 14 September 1829; Disestablished: 1 June 1853

name: Abeokuta
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Abeokuta was a powerful Egba Yoruba city-state established around 1830 beneath the protective granite ramparts of Olumo Rock in south-western Nigeria. Founded by displaced Egba communities fleeing the disintegration of the Oyo Empire, the polity developed a federal system of government uniting distinct township quarters under the collective leadership of the Alake. Abeokuta successfully repelled repeated Dahomean invasions and prospered through palm oil trade with European merchants until British forces established a colonial protectorate in 1894. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Abeokuta; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion and Christianity; Government: Federal traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Alake; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Disestablished: 1894

name: Mayurbhanj State
label: indian princely states
description: Mayurbhanj State was a major princely state in eastern India, covering an expansive territory of forested hills and mineral-rich plains in modern Odisha. Governed from the royal capital of Baripada by the ancient Bhanja Rajput dynasty, the state entered subsidiary treaty relations with the British East India Company in 1829. Mayurbhanj developed advanced judicial systems, iron ore extraction and extensive forestry reserves under British paramountcy before acceding to the Dominion of India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Baripada; Common languages: Odia and Santali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Eastern Ganga dynasty; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Ramdurg State
label: indian princely states
description: Ramdurg State was a Maratha princely state located along the Malaprabha River in northern Karnataka, forming part of the Southern Maratha Country under the Bombay Presidency. Ruled from the fortified town of Ramdurg by the Chitpavan Brahmin Bhave family, the estate had originated as a military fief under the Maratha Peshwas. The rulers exercised domestic civil and fiscal powers under British paramountcy until signing the instrument of accession to the Dominion of India in August 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Ramdurg; Common languages: Kannada and Marathi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: Maratha Empire; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Republic of Ecuador
description: The Republic of Ecuador was founded in May 1830 when the departments of the former Real Audiencia of Quito seceded from the dissolving federation of Gran Colombia. Anchored by its high-altitude capital at Quito and its primary commercial seaport at Guayaquil, the sovereign republic spanned the Pacific coastal plains, the Andean highlands and the upper Amazon basin. The nation established constitutional institutions and integrated the Galápagos Islands into its national territory while surviving recurrent territorial disputes with neighbouring Peru and Colombia. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Quito; Largest city: Guayaquil; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: National Assembly; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 3 May 1830; Preceded by: Gran Colombia

name: French Algeria
description: French Algeria was a major colonial possession established in North Africa following the French military capture of Algiers in July 1830, which overthrew the Ottoman Regency. Governed from the coastal port of Algiers, the colony expanded inland through protracted military campaigns against fierce indigenous resistance led by Emir Abdelkader and local Berber confederacies. Administered initially as a military territory and subsequently partitioned into overseas French departments, colonial rule persisted until the culmination of the Algerian War of Independence in July 1962. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Algiers; Official languages: French; Common languages: Algerian Arabic and Berber languages; Religion: Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor General; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 5 July 1830; Disestablished: 5 July 1962; Succeeded by: Republic of Algeria

name: Kingdom of Belgium
description: The Kingdom of Belgium emerged as an independent European constitutional monarchy following the outbreak of the Belgian Revolution in August 1830, which severed the southern provinces from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Centred at Brussels, the state encompassed both Dutch-speaking Flanders and French-speaking Wallonia, establishing a progressive constitution and installing King Leopold I of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha as its monarch. Recognised internationally as a perpetually neutral power under the 1839 Treaty of London, Belgium became a pioneering industrial nation in continental Europe. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital and largest city: Brussels; Official languages: Dutch, French and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Legislature: Federal Parliament; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 25 August 1830; Preceded by: United Kingdom of the Netherlands

name: Banyo
description: Banyo was an autonomous Fulbe lamidate established in the Adamawa highlands of central Cameroon around 1831 during the regional expansion of the Sokoto Caliphate. Governed by a hereditary Muslim ruler known as the lamido from the fortified town of Banyo, the principality commanded extensive cattle pastures and controlled local trade routes connecting the savanna to the forest zone. The sultanate maintained traditional aristocratic rule over subjugated indigenous communities until German colonial expeditionary forces subdued the town in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign lamidate; Capital: Banyo; Common languages: Fula; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Lamido; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1831; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: German Kamerun

name: Jandol Khanate
description: The Jandol Khanate was a minor Pashtun principality located in the rugged Bajaur and Dir hill country of the north-western frontier of the Indian subcontinent. Governed from the fortified settlement of Barwa by hereditary Tarkani Pashtun chieftains, the state exercised independent control over strategic mountain passes along the Afghan borderlands. The khanate maintained fierce territorial autonomy against neighbouring rival tribes and the rulers of Dir until shifting regional alliances led to its incorporation into the broader Dir state. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Barwa; Common languages: Pashto; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Tribal khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1831; Disestablished: 1860; Succeeded by: Dir State

name: Jimma Abba Jifar
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: Jimma Abba Jifar was a powerful Oromo Muslim kingdom in the fertile Gibe basin of south-western Ethiopia, consolidated under the founding monarch Abba Jifar I in the 1830s. Headquartered at the fortified hill capital of Jiren, the kingdom emerged as the dominant commercial and military power among the Gibe states, prospering through the trade of coffee, civet and gold. The monarchy maintained full sovereign independence until submitting peacefully as an autonomous tributary state to Emperor Menelik II of Ethiopia in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jiren; Common languages: Oromo; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of the Tui Manuʻa
description: The Kingdom of the Tui Manuʻa was a traditional Polynesian paramount chiefdom encompassing the eastern Samoan islands of Taʻu, Ofu and Olosega. Revering an ancient sacred lineage whose paramount titles carried immense cultural and spiritual prestige across Western Polynesia, the realm was governed from the ancestral village of Taʻu. The kingdom preserved sovereign self-rule and strictly regulated foreign trade and mission activities until paramount chief Tui Manuʻa Elisala signed a deed of cession ceding the islands to the United States in February 1900. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Taʻu; Common languages: Samoan; Religion: Traditional Polynesian religion and Christianity; Government: Paramount chiefdom; Ruler title: Tui Manuʻa; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 16 February 1900; Succeeded by: American Samoa

name: Kingdom of Tooro
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Tooro was an autonomous Great Lakes Bantu state in western Uganda that emerged around 1830 when Prince Kaboyo Olimi I seceded from the historic Bunyoro-Kitara Empire. Situated in the shadow of the Rwenzori Mountains with its royal court established near Fort Portal, the realm was inhabited primarily by the Batooro people who maintained rich agro-pastoral traditions. Though briefly reoccupied by Bunyoro armies during the 1870s, Tooro re-established its royal dynasty before coming under British colonial protection in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fort Portal; Common languages: Rutooro; Religion: Traditional African religion and Protestantism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Omukama; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Preceded by: Bunyoro-Kitara

name: Mbokomu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Mbokomu was a traditional Chagga mountain chiefdom situated on the fertile southern slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in north-eastern Tanzania. Centred at the settlement of Mbokomu, the polity relied on intricate gravity-fed irrigation channels to cultivate bananas, yams and coffee while managing terraced agriculture. Governed by a hereditary mangi, the chiefdom engaged in shifting defensive alliances and rivalries with neighbouring Chagga principalities like Moshi until German colonial authorities subjugated the Kilimanjaro kingdoms in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Mbokomu; Common languages: Chagga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chiefdom; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1831; Disestablished: 1891

name: Moshi
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Moshi was a prominent Chagga mountain kingdom established on the volcanic slopes of Mount Kilimanjaro in north-eastern Tanzania. Under the astute leadership of Mangi Rindi and his dynastic successors from the royal village of Moshi, the kingdom established extensive diplomatic and trading contacts with coastal Swahili and Arab caravan merchants. Moshi mobilised disciplined warrior regiments to secure regional dominance among competing Chagga states before German imperial troops conquered the mountain chiefdoms in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Moshi; Common languages: Chagga and Swahili; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Mangi; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1831; Disestablished: 1891

name: Neutral Moresnet
description: Neutral Moresnet was a small European condominium established around the lucrative Vieille Montagne zinc mine at Kelmis, administered jointly by the Kingdom of Prussia and the newly independent Kingdom of Belgium. Formed to resolve border disputes following the dissolution of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, the tiny neutral enclave possessed distinct legal privileges, low taxation and an exemption from military conscription. Governed by two royal commissioners and an appointed mayor, its shared condominium status endured until German imperial unification in 1871 altered Prussia's legal posture. \n\n Status: Neutral condominium; Capital: Kelmis; Common languages: French, German and Limburgish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Joint condominium; Ruler title: Royal Commissioners; Historical era: Modern era; Preceded by: United Kingdom of the Netherlands

name: Soconusco
description: Soconusco was an autonomous frontier region situated along the Pacific coastal plain between south-western Mexico and western Guatemala. Governed from the commercial market town of Tapachula, the territory maintained de facto independence for over a decade while boundary negotiations remained deadlocked between the Mexican Republic and the Federal Republic of Central America. Soconusco prospered from fertile volcanic soils that supported cacao and coffee cultivation until Mexican military forces annexed the district into the State of Chiapas in 1843. \n\n Status: De facto autonomous territory; Capital: Tapachula; Common languages: Spanish and indigenous languages; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Regional self-government; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1831; Disestablished: 1843; Succeeded by: Mexican Republic

name: Sultanate of Dar al-Kuti
description: The Sultanate of Dar al-Kuti was an Islamic state established in the savanna and forest borderlands of northern Central African Republic around 1831. Governed initially from Chá and later from the fortified hilltop citadel of N'Délé, the sultanate maintained lucrative caravan commerce with Wadai and the Chadian basin, trading in ivory and captives. Although nominally subject to larger northern empires, the realm maintained substantial domestic sovereignty under local Muslim dynasts until becoming a French protectorate in August 1897. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: N'Délé; Common languages: Arabic and Banda languages; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Disestablished: 28 August 1897; Succeeded by: French Congo

name: Wahidi Sultanate of Azzan
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Wahidi Sultanate of Azzan was an independent tribal principality located in the rugged wadi valleys of the Hadhramaut region in southern Arabia. Governed from the fortified inland town of Azzan by members of the Al Wahidi dynasty, the state commanded vital caravan junctions linking coastal ports to the Arabian interior. The sultanate maintained traditional sovereign tribal authority and resisted outside hegemony until May 1881, when it formally merged into the neighbouring Wahidi Sultanate of Balhaf. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Azzan; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Al Wahidi; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Disestablished: 4 May 1881; Succeeded by: Wahidi Sultanate of Balhaf

name: Wahidi Sultanate of Balhaf
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Wahidi Sultanate of Balhaf was a sovereign coastal principality situated along the Gulf of Aden in the southern Arabian Peninsula. Headquartered at the historic port town of Balhaf, the sultanate commanded maritime fishing fleets and levied duties on Arabian coastal trade while expanding its inland reach into Azzan. The realm preserved complete political autonomy under its hereditary Wahidi dynasts until 1889, when the sultan concluded a protectorate treaty with Great Britain to join the Aden Protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Balhaf; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Al Wahidi; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Wahidi Sultanate of Bir Ali
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Wahidi Sultanate of Bir Ali was a maritime tribal state situated along the rugged coastline of the Gulf of Aden in southern Yemen. Ruled by a branch of the Al Wahidi lineage from the natural harbour settlement of Bir Ali, the principality oversaw maritime trade, coastal pearling and seasonal date harvesting. The sultanate maintained sovereign self-governance across the nineteenth century until entering into formal protectorate arrangements with the British Crown in 1896. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Bir Ali; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Al Wahidi; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Wahidi Sultanate of Haban
label: southern arabia petty kingdoms
description: The Wahidi Sultanate of Haban was an independent inland principality situated in the high fertile valleys of the southern Arabian Hadhramaut. Governed by hereditary Wahidi sultans from the architecturally celebrated multi-storey mud-brick city of Haban, the state held sway over crucial mountain passes and trade routes. The dynasty preserved its sovereign autonomy and customary tribal administration until 1889, when external geopolitical pressures prompted its rulers to accept British protection under the Aden Protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Haban; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Al Wahidi; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1830; Succeeded by: Aden Protectorate

name: Zemio
description: Zemio was an autonomous Zande principality established along the upper reaches of the Mbomou River in the borderlands of modern-day Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Governed from the riverine settlement of Zemio by hereditary Vungara noblemen, the state incorporated diverse indigenous groups through military organisation and royal patronage. The principality preserved its political independence and managed local hunting and trade networks until 1873, when its rulers transformed the domain into a centralised sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Zemio; Common languages: Zande; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional principality; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1831; Reorganised: 1873

name: Argentine Confederation
description: The Argentine Confederation was a decentralised union of autonomous South American provinces established in January 1831 following the signing of the Federal Pact. Dominated initially by the governor of Buenos Aires, Juan Manuel de Rosas, who conducted foreign relations on behalf of the provinces, the state later established its formal federal capital at Paraná after Buenos Aires seceded in 1852. The Confederation functioned under the 1853 Constitution until its reunification with Buenos Aires in December 1861 formed the unified Argentine Republic. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Buenos Aires (1831-1853), Paraná (1853-1861); Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederation and federal republic; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 4 January 1831; Disestablished: 12 December 1861; Succeeded by: Argentine Republic

name: British Guiana
description: British Guiana was a crown colony situated on the north-eastern coast of South America, formed in July 1831 through the administrative consolidation of Demerara, Essequibo and Berbice. Administered from the coastal capital of Georgetown, the territory developed an economy heavily centred on sugar cane cultivation, bauxite extraction and timber exploitation, supported by emancipated Afro-Guyanese labourers and indentured Indian immigrants. The colony remained a key British imperial outpost on the South American mainland until achieving independence as Guyana in 1966 and declaring a republic in 1970. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Georgetown; Official languages: English; Common languages: Guyanese Creole; Religion: Christianity and Hinduism; Government: Crown colony; Ruler title: Monarch; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 21 July 1831; Succeeded by: Guyana

name: Kingdom of the Netherlands (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of the Netherlands Military Occupation comprised external operational theatres administered by Dutch armed forces during conflicts such as the Belgian campaign of 1831 and subsequent colonial expeditions in Aceh. Operating without a permanent municipal capital, Dutch military commanders exercised martial authority over contested towns and defensive encampments during active hostilities. These temporary occupation administrations maintained logistical control and enforced military law until regular civil governance was established or sovereign peace accords were ratified. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Official languages: Dutch; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Military occupation; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 2 August 1831

name: Republic of New Granada
description: The Republic of New Granada was a sovereign South American state established in November 1831 following the disintegration of Gran Colombia. Centred at Bogotá, the unitary republic encompassed the territories of modern Colombia and Panama along with adjacent border areas. Governed under presidential leadership with intense ideological competition between Liberal and Conservative factions, the country fostered constitutional institutions and commercial expansion until reforming into the federal Granadine Confederation in April 1858. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Bogotá; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 19 November 1831; Disestablished: 11 April 1858; Preceded by: Gran Colombia; Succeeded by: Granadine Confederation

name: State of Venezuela
description: The State of Venezuela was the sovereign successor state in northern South America created after separating definitively from the federation of Gran Colombia in the early 1830s. Headquartered at Caracas under the dominant political and military leadership of General José Antonio Páez, the republic established an agrarian export economy focused on coffee and cacao. Decades of conservative and liberal factional strife culminated in the devastating Federal War, which ultimately led to the proclamation of the United States of Venezuela in the 1860s. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Caracas; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Legislature: Congress; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 19 November 1831; Preceded by: Gran Colombia; Succeeded by: United States of Venezuela

name: Colony of Western Australia
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Colony of Western Australia was an expansive British imperial possession encompassing the western third of the Australian continent, established in February 1832 from the reorganisation of the Swan River Colony. Governed from Perth, the colony expanded inland through agricultural pastoralism, mineral discoveries and convict labour introduced during the mid-nineteenth century. After securing responsible self-government in 1890, Western Australia experienced rapid economic growth during the gold rushes before federating into the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Perth; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Self-governing colony; Ruler title: Governor; Legislature: Parliament of Western Australia; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 6 February 1832; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Australia

name: Republic of Indian Stream
description: The Republic of Indian Stream was a small, unrecognised frontier republic declared on 9 July 1832 along the disputed border separating northern New Hampshire from Lower Canada. Formed by roughly three hundred settlers in response to overlapping tax claims and ambiguous boundary wording from the Treaty of Paris, the community adopted a written constitution and established its own court system. Mounting diplomatic friction and violent cross-border jurisdictional raids prompted New Hampshire militia to occupy the territory in August 1835, ending the enclave's independence. \n\n Status: Unrecognised republic; Capital: Pittsburg; Common languages: English; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Constitutional republic; Ruler title: Justice of the Peace; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 9 July 1832; Disestablished: 5 August 1835; Succeeded by: State of New Hampshire

name: Hellenic State
description: The Hellenic State was an ephemeral transitional polity in south-eastern Europe following the international recognition of Greek independence from the Ottoman Empire under the Treaty of Constantinople in July 1832. Centred provisionally in Athens and Nafplio during the political aftermath of Ioannis Kapodistrias's assassination, the fledgling administration faced severe internal factionalism and financial distress. Its provisional republican institutions functioned for only several weeks before European great powers established the monarchical Kingdom of Greece in late August 1832. \n\n Status: Sovereign state; Capital: Athens; Official languages: Greek; Religion: Greek Orthodoxy; Government: Provisional republic; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 21 July 1832; Disestablished: 30 August 1832; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Greece

name: Kingdom of Greece
description: The Kingdom of Greece was an independent European monarchical state created in August 1832 following the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire. Initially established with its royal court at Nafplio before permanently transferring the capital to Athens in 1834, the kingdom was first ruled by the Bavarian prince Otto of Wittelsbach. Greece evolved from an absolute to a constitutional monarchy while pursuing the Megali Idea to incorporate historic Greek-inhabited lands across the Aegean and Balkans. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Athens; Largest city: Athens; Official languages: Greek; Religion: Greek Orthodoxy; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Legislature: Hellenic Parliament; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 30 August 1832; Preceded by: Hellenic State

name: Emirate of Abdelkader
description: The Emirate of Abdelkader was an independent resistance state founded in western Algeria in November 1832 to defend the indigenous population against French military occupation. Governed by the scholar and military commander Emir Abdelkader from capitals at Mascara and later Tagdemt, the state introduced a centralised Islamic administration, established military manufacturing foundries and minted its own coinage. Abdelkader's disciplined army waged protracted guerrilla warfare across the Tell Atlas until overwhelmed by superior French forces in December 1847. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Mascara and Tagdemt; Official languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic state; Ruler title: Emir; Currency: Muhmadiyya; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 27 November 1832; Disestablished: 23 December 1847; Succeeded by: French Algeria

name: Principality of Samos
description: The Principality of Samos was an autonomous, self-governing Christian principality established on the Aegean island of Samos under Ottoman imperial suzerainty in December 1832. Headquartered at the port town of Vathy, the state was administered by a Greek Christian prince nominated by the Sublime Porte, alongside an elected local parliament and senate. Samos enjoyed substantial commercial and administrative freedom while paying an annual tribute until declaring union with the Kingdom of Greece in November 1912. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Vathy; Common languages: Greek; Religion: Greek Orthodoxy; Government: Tributary constitutional principality; Ruler title: Prince of Samos; Legislature: Parliament of Samos; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 11 December 1832; Disestablished: 24 November 1912; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Greece

name: Agbodrafo
description: Agbodrafo was an autonomous coastal polity situated along the Gulf of Guinea between Lake Togo and the Atlantic Ocean, historically known to European navigators as Porto Seguro. Founded in the 1830s around an older Portuguese fortified station, the town served as a significant regional trading entrepôt inhabited by Gen and Ewe communities as well as returning Afro-Brazilian merchants. The settlement maintained sovereign local governance until German colonial envoy Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty of protection in September 1884. \n\n Status: Sovereign coastal town; Capital: Agbodrafo; Common languages: Ewe and Gen; Religion: Traditional religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional chiefdom; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1833; Disestablished: 5 September 1884; Succeeded by: Togoland

name: Bassa Cove
label: us colonies in liberia
description: Bassa Cove was an American philanthropic settlement colony founded on the Atlantic coast of West Africa near the mouth of the Saint John River. Sponsored jointly by the colonisation societies of Pennsylvania and New York, the colony was settled by emancipated African Americans adhering to pacifist and temperance principles. Governed from the settlement that became Buchanan, Bassa Cove maintained autonomous civil institutions until merging with Monrovia and neighbouring settlements to form the Commonwealth of Liberia in April 1839. \n\n Status: American colonisation colony; Capital: Buchanan; Common languages: English; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1833; Disestablished: 1 April 1839; Succeeded by: Commonwealth of Liberia

name: Edina
label: us colonies in liberia
description: Edina was an early coastal settlement colony established along the mouth of the Saint John River in West Africa in 1833. Founded by the American Colonisation Society and named in honour of financial benefactors in Edinburgh, Scotland, the community was inhabited by freed African-American immigrants and liberated Africans. Edina maintained separate municipal and colonial administration while cultivating trade and defensive cooperation with neighbouring Bassa Cove, into which it formally amalgamated prior to the creation of the Commonwealth of Liberia. \n\n Status: American colonisation colony; Capital: Edina; Common languages: English; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial settlement; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1833; Disestablished: 1838; Succeeded by: Bassa Cove

name: Western Nzima
description: Western Nzima was a sovereign Akan kingdom situated along the south-western coast of modern Ghana, bordering the Tano River and the Gulf of Guinea. Governed from the royal coastal town of Beyin by hereditary paramount rulers known as the Awulae, the state controlled fertile agricultural hinterlands and lucrative regional trade in gold and palm oil. The kingdom fiercely defended its political autonomy against neighbouring chiefdoms and British imperial encroachments until being incorporated into the British Gold Coast Colony in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Beyin; Common languages: Nzema; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Awulae; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1833; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Falkland Islands
description: The Falkland Islands formed a British colonial dependency comprising East Falkland, West Falkland and numerous surrounding South Atlantic islands on the Patagonian Shelf. British imperial authority was permanently reasserted in January 1833, with the administrative capital subsequently established at Stanley. The colony developed a robust pastoral economy based upon extensive sheep farming, wool exportation and naval maritime services. Except for a brief Argentine military occupation in 1982, the islands have remained under British administration as a self-governing overseas territory. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Stanley; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Constitutional dependency; Ruler title: Governor; Legislature: Legislative Assembly; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 2 January 1833

name: Bahawalpur State
label: indian princely states
description: Bahawalpur State was a major Muslim princely state situated along the southern banks of the Sutlej and Indus rivers in the Punjab region. Ruled by the Abbasi Daudpotra dynasty from the desert capital of Bahawalpur, the state entered into a formal subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in February 1833. The nawabs retained internal sovereignty while developing extensive canal irrigation systems that transformed the Cholistan desert into fertile agricultural lands, before acceding to the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Bahawalpur; Common languages: Saraiki, Punjabi and Urdu; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Autocracy; Ruling dynasty: Abbasi; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 22 February 1833; Disestablished: 7 October 1947; Succeeded by: Dominion of Pakistan

name: Heard Island and McDonald Islands
description: Heard Island and McDonald Islands comprised a remote, glaciated subantarctic volcanic archipelago in the southern Indian Ocean claimed as a British imperial dependency. Devoid of an indigenous population or permanent municipal capital, the windswept territory was frequented during the nineteenth century by commercial sealing crews who operated temporary coastal camps. The islands served as an isolated station for maritime exploration and scientific observation until Great Britain formally transferred sovereign title over the external territory to the Commonwealth of Australia in December 1947. \n\n Status: British dependency; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English; Government: Colonial dependency; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 27 November 1833; Disestablished: 26 December 1947; Succeeded by: Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands

name: Khairagarh State
label: indian princely states
description: Khairagarh State was an Indian princely state situated in the Chota Nagpur plateau and modern Chhattisgarh region, ruled by the Nagvanshi Gond Rajput dynasty. Administered from its capital at Khairagarh town, the state commanded fertile agricultural plains bordered by densely forested hills. Its hereditary rajas exercised internal civil and revenue administration under the supervision of the Eastern States Agency of British India until signing the instrument of accession to merge into the Republic of India in 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Khairagarh; Common languages: Chhattisgarhi and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Nagvanshi; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1833; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Peki
description: Peki was a sovereign Ewe traditional kingdom situated in the scenic inland valleys of the Volta Region in south-eastern Ghana. Governed from the ancestral settlement of Peki by a paramount ruler bearing the title of Deiga, the polity united eight historic subtowns through a well-ordered confederate council. The kingdom defended its independence against expansionist Ashanti invasions and regional Akwamu rivalries across the nineteenth century before being incorporated into the British Gold Coast protectorate in 1902. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Peki; Common languages: Ewe; Religion: Traditional African religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Deiga; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1834; Disestablished: 1902; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Principality of Svaneti
description: The Principality of Svaneti was an autonomous mountain principality nestled within the high valleys of the Greater Caucasus in north-western Georgia. Ruled by the Dadeshkeliani princely dynasty from strongholds around Mestia, the state accepted nominal Russian imperial protectorate status in 1834 while retaining virtually undisturbed feudal autonomy. Escalating friction with imperial administrators culminated in 1857 when Prince Konstantine Dadeshkeliani assassinated the Russian governor of Kutaisi, prompting imperial authorities to execute the prince and fully annex Svaneti. \n\n Status: Russian protectorate; Capital: Mestia; Common languages: Svan and Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Dadeshkeliani; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1834; Disestablished: 1858; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Colony of Maryland in Liberia
label: us colonies in liberia
description: The Colony of Maryland in Liberia was an American settlement established at Cape Palmas in February 1834 by the Maryland State Colonisation Society. Governed from the coastal town of Harper, the colony accommodated emancipated and freeborn African Americans from the state of Maryland, operating independently of the American Colonisation Society in Monrovia. The settlement cultivated cash crops and conducted coastal trade while defending its perimeter against local Grebo populations, eventually declaring independence as the Republic of Maryland in May 1854. \n\n Status: American colonisation colony; Capital: Harper; Common languages: English and Grebo; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 12 February 1834; Disestablished: 29 May 1854; Succeeded by: Republic of Maryland

name: Jafarabad State
label: indian princely states
description: Jafarabad State was a maritime princely dependency situated on the southern coast of the Kathiawar Peninsula in Gujarat, held in dynastic union with Janjira State. Ruled by an African-descended Habshi Siddi dynasty from the fortified port town of Jafrabad, the enclave comprised eleven coastal villages around the Ranai river estuary. The rulers exercised local judicial and administrative powers under the supervision of the Kathiawar Agency of British India until the principality merged into independent India in August 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jafrabad; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Siddi dynasty; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1835; Disestablished: 3 August 1948; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Owu
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Owu was a prominent Yoruba kingdom reconstituted in south-western Nigeria around 1835 following the catastrophic sack and dispersal of its ancient capital at Orile Owu. Led by war chiefs and royal elders who relocated to the fortified confederacy of Abeokuta, the community established the influential quarter of Ago-Owu while retaining its distinct crown, titled chieftaincies and military institutions. Owu maintained vibrant commercial and military roles in regional Yoruba affairs until the British established formal colonial control over the region in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Abeokuta; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Olowu; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1835; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Lagos Colony

name: Togo
description: Togo was an autonomous precolonial Ewe polity situated along the northern shores of Lake Togo and the nearby Bight of Benin coastline in West Africa. Centred at the sacred lakeside town of Togoville with trading outposts extending toward the fishing village of Lomé, the state prospered as an intermediary hub for regional agricultural produce and maritime commerce. The local ruler, King Mlapa III, exercised traditional authority over the surrounding communities until signing a historic protectorate treaty with the German Empire on 6 July 1884. \n\n Status: Sovereign traditional kingdom; Capital: Lomé; Common languages: Ewe and Gen; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1835; Disestablished: 6 July 1884; Succeeded by: Togoland

name: Usangu
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: Usangu was a powerful Great Lakes kingdom established by the Sangu people across the expansive Usangu Plain and Southern Highlands of south-central Tanzania. Governed from the formidable stone-walled fortress of Utengule by paramount chiefs of the Merere lineage, the state dominated major caravan routes connecting the East African interior to the Swahili coast. The Sangu kingdom maintained a standing warrior army to resist persistent incursions by neighbouring Hehe forces before falling under German colonial rule in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Utengule; Common languages: Sangu and Swahili; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Chief; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1835; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: German East Africa

name: Cabanagem Rebels
description: The Cabanagem Rebels formed a revolutionary insurgent government that controlled extensive riverine territories in the northern Brazilian province of Grão-Pará between January 1835 and 1841. Originating from an alliance of impoverished river dwellers, indigenous peoples, freed slaves and radical mestizo leaders against imperial Brazilian dominance, the rebels captured the provincial capital of Belém and established provisional administrations. Operating across Amazonian waterways without a fixed administrative centre, the uprising resisted imperial military pacification campaigns for six years before being ruthlessly suppressed. \n\n Status: Revolutionary rebel government; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Portuguese and Nheengatu; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary council; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 6 January 1835; Disestablished: 1841; Succeeded by: Empire of Brazil

name: League of the Three Cities
description: The League of the Three Cities was an armed confederacy formed in September 1835 by the Costa Rican municipalities of Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago during the League War. Formed in response to the repeal of the rotating capital law, the coalition sought to prevent San José from permanently establishing itself as the national seat of government. Operating without a unified administrative capital, the league's provincial militias engaged government troops across the Central Valley until their decisive military defeat at the Battle of Cuesta de Moras in October 1835. \n\n Status: Insurgent confederacy; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal alliance; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 25 September 1835; Disestablished: 28 October 1835; Succeeded by: Republic of Costa Rica

name: Provisional Government of Texas
description: The Provisional Government of Texas was a revolutionary administrative authority established by Texian and Tejano colonists following the outbreak of hostilities against the centralist Mexican Republic in October 1835. Organised through the Consultation convention and guided by the General Council, the provisional regime raised volunteer regiments, appointed Sam Houston as commander of the regular army and asserted loyalty to the federal Mexican Constitution of 1824. The itinerant wartime authority directed military operations until delegates formally proclaimed the independent Republic of Texas on 2 March 1836. \n\n Status: Provisional revolutionary government; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: English and Spanish; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional government; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 2 October 1835; Disestablished: 2 March 1836; Succeeded by: Republic of Texas

name: Mexican Republic
description: The Mexican Republic was a unitary constitutional regime established in October 1835 following the repeal of the federal 1824 Constitution and the enactment of the conservative Seven Laws. Administered from Mexico City under the alternating leadership of Antonio López de Santa Anna and Anastasio Bustamante, the state dismantled provincial state legislatures and concentrated political authority within the national executive. The regime contended with intense regional rebellions in Texas, Yucatán and the Rio Grande until the outbreak of the Mexican-American War prompted the restoration of the federal republic in 1846. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Mexico City; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Legislature: Congress; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 23 October 1835; Disestablished: 22 August 1846; Succeeded by: United Mexican States

name: United Tribes of New Zealand
description: The United Tribes of New Zealand was an indigenous Māori tribal confederation formed in October 1835 when thirty-four northern rangatira signed the Declaration of Independence at Waitangi. Convening regular congresses without a permanent municipal capital, the confederation asserted collective sovereignty over the northern North Island and received formal diplomatic acknowledgement from the British Crown. name: Colony of Mississippi-in-Africa

name: Kingdom of Gera

description: The Kingdom of Gera was an autonomous Oromo monarchy established in the forested Gibe River basin of south-western Ethiopia. Ruled from the royal hilltop settlement of Chala by hereditary kings bearing the title of Donacho, the state prospered through fertile soil, wild coffee harvesting and trade with neighbouring Limmu-Ennarea and Jimma. name: Loharu State
label: indian princely states
description: Loharu State was a small Muslim princely state situated in the arid borderlands between south-eastern Punjab and Rajasthan. Ruled by nawabs of the Mughal Mirza dynasty from the fortified town of Loharu, the principality maintained close literary and cultural ties with Delhi, being famously linked to the renowned poet Mirza Ghalib. name: Mongkung State
label: shan states
description: Mongkung State was an autonomous Shan principality situated in the lush valley of the Nam Teng River in the eastern highlands of Burma. Governed by a hereditary Shan sawbwa from the central town of Mong Kung, the state functioned as a tributary vassal to the Konbaung dynasty of the Burmese Empire. name: Republic of Zoutpansberg
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Zoutpansberg was an isolated frontier Boer republic established in the far northern reaches of the Transvaal around the Soutpansberg mountain range. Centred on the fortified trading settlement of Schoemansdal, the community was founded by Voortrekker emigrants led by Hendrik Potgieter who engaged extensively in ivory hunting and regional bartering with Venda and Pedi chiefdoms. name: Province of South Australia

description: The Province of South Australia was a British colonial possession established along the southern coast of Australia under the South Australia Act of 1834. Planned according to the systematic colonisation theories of Edward Gibbon Wakefield to promote free immigrant settlement without convict transportation, the colony established its surveyed capital at Adelaide. The province developed a thriving agricultural and copper mining economy, instituted democratic parliamentary self-government in 1857 and remained a self-governing dependency until joining the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901. \n\n Status: British crown colony; Capital: Adelaide; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Self-governing colony; Ruler title: Governor; Legislature: Parliament of South Australia; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 19 February 1836; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: State of South Australia

name: Republic of Texas
description: The Republic of Texas was a sovereign North American state established on 2 March 1836 following the Texian Declaration of Independence from the centralist Mexican Republic. Securing its borders after the decisive victory at the Battle of San Jacinto, the republic established its permanent government at Austin under presidents such as Sam Houston and Mirabeau B. Lamar. Texas navigated diplomatic recognition from European powers, continuous border skirmishes with Mexico and domestic debt before formally consenting to annexation by the United States in December 1845. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Austin; Common languages: English and Spanish; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Legislature: Congress of the Republic of Texas; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 2 March 1836; Disestablished: 29 December 1845; Succeeded by: United States of America

name: Territory of Wisconsin

name: Riograndense Republic

Sparked by grievances over imperial taxation and regional marginalisation during the Ragamuffin War, the republic established its primary capital at Piratini under President Bento Gonçalves. name: Peru-Bolivian Confederation
description: The Peru-Bolivian Confederation was a short-lived South American union established in October 1836 under the leadership of Supreme Protector Andrés de Santa Cruz. Uniting the Republic of North Peru, the Republic of South Peru and the Republic of Bolivia into a single confederated polity, the government maintained its central administrative institutions between Tacna and Lima. name: Basotho Kingdom

Uniting fragmented Sotho clans who had fled the violent dislocations of the Mfecane, the kingdom established administrative centres across the fertile Caledon River valley around Maseru. Moshoeshoe employed astute diplomacy with European missionaries and Boer trekkers while maintaining a skilled equestrian cavalry to safeguard the nation, laying the direct institutional foundation for modern Lesotho. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Maseru; Common languages: Sesotho; Religion: Traditional African religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1837; Disestablished: 1844; Succeeded by: Basutoland

name: Emirate of Jabal Shammar
description: The Emirate of Jabal Shammar was a powerful tribal monarchy in the northern Nejd region of the Arabian Peninsula, established under the leadership of the Al Rashid dynasty. name: Ijaye

Ruled autocratically by the warlord Kurunmi, who assumed the traditional title of Aare Ona Kakanfo from the settlement of Ijaye, the polity became a major martial haven for refugees and a regional powerbroker. name: N'Gaoundere
description: N'Gaoundere was an autonomous Fulbe lamidate established on the high Adamawa Plateau of central Cameroon around 1837 under the leadership of Ardo Ndjobdi. Centred at the fortified town of Ngaoundéré beneath its eponymous granite mountain, the state served as a vital commercial nexus for ivory, cattle rearing and regional caravan routes connecting the Lake Chad basin with the southern forests. name: Kingdom of Hanover

name: Republic of Chile (Military Occupation)
description: The Republic of Chile Military Occupation encompassed external territories administered under martial law by the Chilean armed forces during regional conflicts in western South America. name: Republic of Canada

name: Republic of Nicaragua
description: The Republic of Nicaragua became a fully sovereign Central American nation on 31 May 1838 after formally seceding from the collapsing Federal Republic of Central America. Initially plagued by bitter rivalries between the liberal capital of León and the conservative stronghold of Granada, the republic eventually established a compromise capital at Managua in the 1850s. name: Territory of Iowa
description: The Territory of Iowa was an organised incorporated territory of the United States formed in July 1838 from lands west of the Mississippi River previously administered under the Wisconsin Territory. Governed initially from Burlington and subsequently from the purpose-built territorial capital at Iowa City, the administration directed land surveys and settlement across rich prairie farmlands. name: Republic of Honduras
