Governed initially from the colonial capital of Comayagua before permanently transferring the seat of government to the mining city of Tegucigalpa, the country was shaped by persistent conflicts between Liberal and Conservative elites. name: Pitcairn Islands

Inhabited by the descendants of the HMS Bounty mutineers and their Polynesian companions in the hillside village of Adamstown, the community adopted a pioneering legal code that notably granted universal suffrage to adult women. The islanders sustained a communal agrarian and seafaring lifestyle under the pastoral guidance of local magistrates and periodic visits from Royal Navy vessels throughout the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: British colony; Capital: Adamstown; Common languages: Pitkern and English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Island council dependency; Ruler title: Magistrate; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 30 November 1838

name: Commonwealth of Liberia

name: Emirate of Nasarawa
description: The Emirate of Nasarawa was a traditional Muslim principality established in central Nigeria around 1839 by Umaru, a renowned commander from Keffi who had pledged fealty to the Emir of Zaria. Governed from the newly fortified town of Nasarawa, the state expanded through military campaigns across the fertile Benue river valley, bringing diverse indigenous agricultural communities under its fiscal control. The emirate preserved its dynastic succession and local administrative independence until British colonial expeditionary forces subdued the region in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Nasarawa; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1839; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Jhalawar State

Created by treaty with the British East India Company to reward the descendants of the influential regent Zalim Singh Jhala, the state was governed from the royal residence at Jhalawar and the thriving commercial hub of Jhalrapatan. The Jhala Rajput dynasty ruled over fertile agricultural plains and maintained a fifteen-gun salute until administrative reorganisations led to its temporary restructuring in 1898. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Jhalawar; Common languages: Hadoti and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jhala; Ruler title: Maharaj Rana; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1838; Disestablished: 1898; Preceded by: Kotah State

name: Khairpur State

description: Khairpur State was a princely state in northern Sindh along the eastern banks of the Indus River, ruled by the Talpur Baloch dynasty from the palace city of Khairpur. Entering into subsidiary treaty arrangements with the British East India Company in 1838 and 1839, the state preserved its domestic autonomy when the rest of Sindh was conquered by British forces in 1843. The Talpur mirs maintained internal civil administration, patronised Islamic scholarship and developed modern irrigation canals until acceding to the Dominion of Pakistan in August 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Khairpur; Common languages: Sindhi and Balochi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Talpur; Ruler title: Mir; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1783; Disestablished: 14 August 1947; Succeeded by: Dominion of Pakistan

name: Republic of Costa Rica
description: The Republic of Costa Rica emerged as an independent sovereign nation following the collapse of the Federal Republic of Central America in 1838 and the assumption of dictatorial powers by Braulio Carrillo in 1839. Anchored by its capital at San José in the fertile Central Valley, the country developed an agrarian export economy driven by coffee cultivation and international trade. Costa Rica cultivated robust democratic institutions, transitioned peacefully to constitutional governance and later famously abolished its standing military in 1948, establishing an enduring tradition of civilian rule. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: San José; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Legislative Assembly; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1839; Preceded by: Federal Republic of Central America

name: Republic of Potchefstroom
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Potchefstroom was an early Boer republic founded along the Mooi River in the south-western Transvaal in 1839 by Voortrekker leader Andries Hendrik Potgieter. Serving as the primary political and agricultural hub for emigrant burghers north of the Vaal River, the town of Potchefstroom housed the community's elected Volksraad and judicial offices. The state maintained armed commandos to defend its pastoral lands against local African kingdoms before formally unifying with its southern neighbour to form the Republic of Winburg-Potchefstroom in the mid-1840s. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Potchefstroom; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Calvinism; Government: Boer republic; Ruler title: Commandant-General; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1839; Disestablished: 1845; Succeeded by: Republic of Winburg-Potchefstroom

name: Aden Protectorate

Supervised initially by the Bombay Presidency and administered from coastal headquarters near Little Aden, the protectorate comprised dozens of autonomous tribal sultanates, emirates and sheikhdoms who entered protective treaty relationships with the British Crown. The traditional rulers retained broad domestic sovereignty and customary law until British authorities reorganised the territories into South Arabian federations in 1963. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Administrative seat: Little Aden; Common languages: Arabic and English; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Colonial protectorate; Ruler title: British Resident; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 19 January 1839; Disestablished: 18 January 1963; Succeeded by: Protectorate of South Arabia

name: Duchy of Limburg
label: confederation of the rhine;german confederation
description: The Duchy of Limburg was a European territory created in April 1839 under the Treaty of London to compensate the German Confederation for the loss of western Luxembourg to Belgium. Held in personal union by King William I of the Netherlands and his successors as Dukes of Limburg, the province was administered from Maastricht while simultaneously functioning as an integral Dutch province and a member state of the German Confederation. This dual international status persisted until the 1867 Treaty of London formally dissolved the duchy's confederal obligations. \n\n Status: Ducal state in personal union; Capital: Maastricht; Common languages: Dutch, Limburgish and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: German Confederation; Established: 19 April 1839; Disestablished: 11 May 1867; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Netherlands

name: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg
label: german confederation
description: The Grand Duchy of Luxembourg emerged with its modern national borders on 19 April 1839 following the Treaty of London, which partitioned the historic territory by transferring its western Francophone districts to Belgium. Governed from the fortified city of Luxembourg, the remaining Germanic and Luxembourgish-speaking grand duchy remained in personal union under the King of the Netherlands and garrisoned by Prussian troops within the German Confederation. The country attained complete dynastic independence under the House of Nassau-Weilburg in 1890, evolving into a prosperous constitutional democracy. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand duchy; Capital and largest city: Luxembourg; Official languages: Luxembourgish, French and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Duke; Legislature: Chamber of Deputies; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 19 April 1839

name: Kingdom of the Netherlands

Governed from the constitutional capital of Amsterdam with the royal court and parliament seated at The Hague, the state transitioned under King William II and the 1848 constitutional revisions into a progressive parliamentary democracy. The maritime nation expanded its global trade networks and overseas colonial empire in the East and West Indies across the modern era. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Amsterdam; Administrative seat: The Hague; Official languages: Dutch; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: Monarch; Legislature: States General; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 19 April 1839

name: Yucatecan Rebels

Commanded by federalist militia captain Santiago Imán from jungle encampments in Tizimín without a permanent civil capital, the rebellion mobilised indigenous Maya recruits by promising land reforms and tax relief. The rebel forces swiftly captured the regional garrisons of Valladolid and Mérida, ultimately expelling Mexican federal troops and paving the way for the proclamation of the independent Republic of Yucatán. \n\n Status: Insurgent rebel movement; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish and Yucatec Maya; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary council; Ruler title: Commander; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 2 May 1839; Disestablished: 1 March 1840; Succeeded by: Republic of Yucatán

name: Free and Independent Catarinense Republic
description: The Free and Independent Catarinense Republic, commonly known as the Juliana Republic, was a short-lived revolutionary state proclaimed on 29 July 1839 in the southern Brazilian province of Santa Catarina. Established when Gaúcho rebel forces under General David Canabarro and Italian volunteer Giuseppe Garibaldi captured the coastal port of Laguna during the Ragamuffin War, the republic sought to forge a federal union with the neighbouring Riograndense Republic. Brazilian imperial naval forces blockaded the port and recaptured Laguna in November 1839, dissolving the rebel government. \n\n Status: Unrecognised republic; Capital: Laguna; Common languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 29 July 1839; Disestablished: 15 November 1839; Succeeded by: Empire of Brazil

name: Emirate of Afghanistan
description: The Emirate of Afghanistan was a Central Asian mountain state that operated under British imperial protectorate status following the British invasion and capture of Kabul in August 1839 during the First Anglo-Afghan War. Administered from Kabul where British political envoys installed the restored monarch Shah Shujah Durrani under the protection of imperial garrison troops, the protectorate provoked widespread tribal rebellion across the Hindu Kush. Fierce national resistance culminated in January 1842 with the disastrous British retreat from Kabul, temporarily eliminating British political control in the region. \n\n Status: British protectorate; Capital: Kabul; Common languages: Pashto and Dari Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy under military protectorate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Great Game; Established: 3 August 1839; Disestablished: 13 January 1842

name: Khanate of Khiva (Military Occupation)
description: The Khanate of Khiva Military Occupation encompassed desolate desert operational sectors across the Ustyurt Plateau and Karakum borderlands mobilised by Khivan forces during the Russian Khivan Campaign of 1839 to 1840. Commanded by Uzbek and Turkmen cavalry officers without a fixed administrative capital, the forces deployed mobile skirmishing parties to intercept and harass the invading Russian expeditionary column under General Vasily Perovsky. Severe winter blizzards and devastating logistical collapse decimated the Russian army, compelling the invaders to retreat and leaving Khivan frontier authority intact. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Chagatai and Turkmen; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military command; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 30 December 1839; Disestablished: 2 January 1840

name: Ahanta Kingdom
description: The Ahanta Kingdom was a traditional coastal Akan state situated along the Gold Coast of south-western Ghana that fell under Dutch imperial protectorate status in 1840 following the suppression of King Badu Bonsu II's rebellion. Governed from the coastal royal seat of Busua and supervised from Dutch headquarters at Fort Batenstein and Fort Elmina, the kingdom engaged in lucrative palm oil trade and artisanal gold extraction. The territory remained under Dutch colonial protection until the Netherlands ceded its Gold Coast forts and protectorates to Great Britain in 1872. \n\n Status: Dutch protectorate; Capital: Busua; Common languages: Ahanta and Fante; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Established: 1840; Disestablished: 1872; Succeeded by: Gold Coast

name: Baghat State
label: indian princely states
description: Baghat State was one of the Simla Hill States situated across the rugged lower Himalayan ranges of present-day Himachal Pradesh in northern India. Ruled by a dynasty of Rajput rajas from ancestral seats at Jaunaji and later the hill station of Solan, the principality experienced periods of escheat under the Doctrine of Lapse before being restored to native dynasts. The rulers exercised internal civil and judicial administration under the Punjab Hill States Agency of the British Raj until acceding to the Indian Union in April 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Solan; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1840; Disestablished: 15 April 1948; Succeeded by: Republic of India

name: Kingdom of Kubang Pasu Darul Qiyam
description: The Kingdom of Kubang Pasu Darul Qiyam was a Malay monarchical state established in the northern Malay Peninsula around 1839 as an autonomous reward granted to nobleman Tunku Anum for mediating peace between Kedah and Siam. Governed from royal residences at Pulau Pisang near modern Jitra, the kingdom operated as a tributary client of the Siamese Kingdom of Rattanakosin while managing local rice agriculture and riverine trade. Following the deaths of its two successive rulers, the realm was peacefully re-integrated into the Sultanate of Kedah in November 1864. \n\n Status: Autonomous kingdom; Capital: Jitra; Common languages: Kedah Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kedahan royal house; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Modern era; Established: 1839; Disestablished: 10 November 1864; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Kedah

name: Kingdom of Shewa
description: The Kingdom of Shewa was a powerful Amhara monarchy situated across the central Ethiopian highlands, serving as a dynamic centre of political expansion and Christian cultural life. Governed by illustrious monarchs including King Sahle Selassie and later King Menelik II, who founded the capital of Addis Ababa, the kingdom maintained a formidable military and established direct diplomatic missions with European powers. Shewa maintained sovereign autonomy through the Era of the Princes until Menelik II was crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in March 1889, uniting the realm into the Ethiopian Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Addis Ababa; Common languages: Amharic; Religion: Ethiopian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Solomonic dynasty; Ruler title: Negus; Historical era: Modern era; Disestablished: 10 March 1889; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Makran State
label: indian princely states
description: Makran State was an autonomous princely state located in the arid, mountainous coastal region of south-western Balochistan. Ruled by hereditary nawabs of the Gichki dynasty from their administrative seat at Turbat and Kech, the state concluded subsidiary treaty arrangements with British Indian authorities during the mid-nineteenth century while retaining extensive internal jurisdiction. The principality preserved its traditional tribal institutions and maritime trading links along the Arabian Sea until formally acceding to the newly independent Dominion of Pakistan in March 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Turbat; Common languages: Balochi and Brahui; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gichki; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1840; Disestablished: 17 March 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of Pakistan

name: Republic of the Rio Grande
description: The Republic of the Rio Grande was a short-lived breakaway federalist state declared by northern Mexican insurgents in opposition to the centralist regime of Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna. Led by figures such as Jesus de Cardenas and Antonio Canales Rosillo, the provisional administration organised resistance across Coahuila, Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas from headquarters at Guerrero. The insurrection collapsed in November 1840 following military engagements and a negotiated surrender to central government forces. \n\n Status: Provisional insurgent republic; Administrative seat: Guerrero; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional junta; Head of state: Jesus de Cardenas; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Mexican federalist conflicts; Established: 17 January 1840; Disestablished: 6 November 1840; Succeeded by: Centralist Republic of Mexico

name: Republic of Natalia
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Natalia was a short-lived Boer republic established in south-eastern Africa by Voortrekkers following their victory over the Zulu at the Battle of Blood River. Governed by a representative Volksraad with its capital at Pietermaritzburg, the state sought diplomatic recognition while maintaining uneasy relations with both indigenous neighbours and British authorities. Persistent conflict and British maritime pressure culminated in military annexation in May 1843, prompting many settlers to trek further inland. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Pietermaritzburg; Common languages: Dutch and Zulu; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Republic; Legislature: Volksraad; Historical era: The Great Trek; Established: 29 January 1840; Disestablished: 4 May 1843; Succeeded by: Colony of Natal

name: Bemazava Kingdom
description: The Bemazava Kingdom was a Sakalava royal domain situated along the north-western coastline of Madagascar that accepted French suzerainty to counter expansionist pressure from the central Merina monarchy. Governed by hereditary Sakalava monarchs from its royal settlement at Bemazava, the kingdom maintained internal autonomy while granting maritime and commercial concessions to French colonial representatives. This protectorate arrangement lasted until France consolidated its direct rule across the entire island in 1897. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Bemazava; Common languages: Malagasy and French; Religion: Traditional Malagasy beliefs; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Madagascar; Established: 14 July 1840; Disestablished: 28 February 1897; Succeeded by: Malagasy Protectorate

name: Colony of New Zealand
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Colony of New Zealand was a British Crown dependency established across the North and South islands following the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi and formal separation from New South Wales. Administrative headquarters shifted sequentially from Okiato to Auckland before settling permanently at Wellington in 1865. The colony transitioned from direct gubernatorial rule to parliamentary responsible government during the 1850s, eventually attaining dominion status within the British Empire in September 1907. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Wellington; Common languages: English and Maori; Religion: Christianity; Government: Parliamentary constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: British monarch; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Victorian era; Established: 16 November 1840; Disestablished: 26 September 1907; Succeeded by: Dominion of New Zealand

name: Chiefdom of Kokang
label: shan states
description: The Chiefdom of Kokang was a mountainous border principality located in the northern Shan hills of modern Myanmar, administered by hereditary Han Chinese chieftains of the Yang clan under Qing imperial suzerainty. Governed from its seat at Laukkai, the polity acted as a tributary buffer state between Upper Burma and Yunnan while preserving extensive local customary autonomy. Imperial Chinese overlordship persisted until the demarcation of Anglo-Chinese frontier agreements in 1897 transferred Kokang into the British sphere. \n\n Status: Tributary chiefdom of the Qing Empire; Capital: Laukkai; Common languages: Southwestern Mandarin and Shan; Religion: Chinese folk religion and Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Yang clan; Historical era: Qing dynasty; Established: 1841; Reorganised: 4 February 1897; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Free State of the Isthmus
description: The Free State of the Isthmus was an ephemeral independent republic proclaimed in November 1840 when General Tomas de Herrera separated the provinces of Panama and Veraguas from the Republic of New Granada. Centred in Panama City, the provisional government drafted an organic constitution and established commercial ties with neighbouring nations to safeguard regional stability amid ongoing Colombian civil conflicts. After negotiating favourable terms of political reintegration with New Granadan authorities, the leaders peacefully dissolved the separate state in early 1842. \n\n Status: Unrecognised republic; Capital: Panama City; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Republic; Head of state: Tomas de Herrera; Historical era: Post-Gran Colombia period; Established: 1841; Disestablished: 1842; Preceded by: Republic of New Granada; Succeeded by: Republic of New Granada

name: Kingdom of Mthwakazi
description: The Kingdom of Mthwakazi was a powerful Northern Ndebele state established in the Matabeleland highveld of modern Zimbabwe by King Mzilikazi after leading his followers away from Zulu dominion. Governed from royal capitals near Bulawayo, the polity integrated diverse local Shona and Rozvi populations into an organised militarised society structured around age-set regiments. Under King Lobengula, the realm resisted European encroachment until British South Africa Company forces overran its forces during the First Matabele War in late 1893. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bulawayo; Common languages: Northern Ndebele and Shona; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Khumalo; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1841; Disestablished: 1 December 1893; Succeeded by: Company rule in Rhodesia

name: Nandi
description: The Nandi polity was an autonomous highland society in the western Rift Valley of modern Kenya, organised around decentralised territorial sections and age-grade warrior regiments. Supreme ritual and political guidance resided in the prophetic office of the orkoiyot, with community coordination anchored near modern Kapsabet. The fierce martial cohesion of the Nandi warriors enabled them to control vital trade routes and resist neighbouring pastoralists until increasing British colonial incursions began in the late 1880s. \n\n Status: Sovereign traditional polity; Administrative seat: Kapsabet; Common languages: Nandi and Kalenjin; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Decentralised tribal confederation; Ruler title: Orkoiyot; Historical era: Precolonial East Africa; Established: 1841; Reorganised: 1889; Succeeded by: East Africa Protectorate

name: Wukari Federation
description: The Wukari Federation was a traditional Jukun state located in the middle Benue River basin of present-day eastern Nigeria, carrying forward the royal traditions of the ancient Kwararafa confederacy. Governed from the town of Wukari by a divine king titled the Aku Uka, the federation exercised spiritual authority and diplomatic influence over surrounding agricultural communities. The polity maintained its sovereignty against Sokoto jihadist incursions throughout the mid-nineteenth century before accepting British protection under the Royal Niger Company in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederation; Capital: Wukari; Common languages: Jukun; Religion: Traditional Jukun religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Aku Uka; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1841; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Northern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Colony of Hong Kong
label: concessions in china
description: The Colony of Hong Kong was a British Crown colony established along the southern coast of China following its naval occupation during the First Opium War and formal cession under the 1842 Treaty of Nanking. Administered from Victoria City on Hong Kong Island, the territory subsequently expanded through the 1860 acquisition of Kowloon and the 1898 lease of the New Territories. It developed into a prominent global entrepot and financial centre before being returned to Chinese sovereignty on 1 July 1997. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Victoria; Official languages: English and Cantonese; Religion: Buddhism, Taoism and Christianity; Government: Crown colony; Ruler title: British monarch; Representative title: Governor; Currency: Hong Kong dollar; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 26 January 1841; Disestablished: 1 July 1997; Succeeded by: Hong Kong Special Administrative Region

name: Republic of El Salvador
description: The Republic of El Salvador emerged as a sovereign Central American nation in February 1841 following the final collapse of the Federal Republic of Central America. Governed from the historic capital of San Salvador, the young republic navigated decades of regional strife, border disputes and internal conflicts between liberal and conservative factions. Its economy became heavily orientated towards commercial indigo and coffee cultivation as state institutions and constitutional governance gradually matured throughout the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: San Salvador; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Legislature: Legislative Assembly; Historical era: Post-colonial Central America; Established: 18 February 1841; Currency: Salvadoran peso

name: Republic of Yucatán
description: The Republic of Yucatán was a breakaway federalist state declared on the Yucatan Peninsula in March 1841 to protest against the centralist policies of the Mexican government. Centred at Merida, the republic instituted a progressive constitution guaranteeing civil liberties, religious tolerance and legal protection through the writ of amparo. However, the outbreak of the catastrophic Caste War with indigenous Maya communities forced regional leaders to seek military assistance from Mexico City in exchange for rejoining the Mexican federation in August 1848. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Merida; Common languages: Spanish and Yucatec Maya; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal republic; Ruler title: President; Historical era: Nineteenth-century Mexico; Established: 16 March 1841; Disestablished: 17 August 1848; Preceded by: Centralist Republic of Mexico; Succeeded by: Second Federal Republic of Mexico

name: Colony of Mayotte

description: The Colony of Mayotte was a French insular possession in the northern Mozambique Channel, established after Sultan Andriantsoly ceded the island to French naval representatives under the Treaty of April 1841. Administered initially from the fortified islet of Dzaoudzi before expanding civil institutions to Mamoudzou, the colony functioned as a strategic maritime station and sugar plantation outpost. French administrators gradually extended their political oversight over neighbouring Comorian sultanates, incorporating Mayotte into broader colonial administrative structures by 1922. \n\n Status: French colony; Administrative seat: Dzaoudzi; Common languages: French, Comorian and Malagasy; Religion: Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: French monarch; Historical era: French colonial expansion; Established: 1 May 1841; Reorganised: 1922; Succeeded by: Colony of Madagascar and Dependencies

name: Sikh Empire (Military Occupation)
description: The Sikh Empire (Military Occupation) denotes the operational field territory controlled by the Khalsa army and Dogra forces under General Zorawar Singh during the Himalayan military campaign into western Tibet. Operating without a permanent civilian administrative capital, the invading expeditionary garrisons occupied strategic monasteries and trade posts across the high-altitude plateau near Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar. name: State of Sarawak

Administered from Kuching, the realm became famous as the domain of the White Rajahs, who steadily suppressed coastal piracy and expanded their borders across interior river basins. name: French Congo

name: Colony of Ivory Coast

Officially proclaimed a distinct colony in 1893, its administrative centre was relocated to Bingerville and eventually to the burgeoning port city of Abidjan in the 1930s. The colony transformed into a major agricultural producer of cocoa and coffee prior to gaining complete national independence under Felix Houphouet-Boigny in August 1960. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Abidjan; Official languages: French; Common languages: French, Baoule, Bete and Dyula; Religion: Islam, Christianity and traditional faiths; Government: Colonial administration; Currency: West African CFA franc; Historical era: French West Africa; Established: 10 February 1842; Disestablished: 7 August 1960; Succeeded by: Republic of Ivory Coast

name: French Polynesia

Headquartered at Papeete on the island of Tahiti, French colonial authorities exercised increasing oversight over traditional Polynesian monarchs through resident commissioners and military garrisons. This fragmented system of protectorates gradually consolidated into a formal overseas colonial entity known as the French Establishments in Oceania in December 1880. \n\n Status: French overseas colony; Capital: Papeete; Common languages: French and Tahitian; Religion: Protestantism, Roman Catholicism and traditional beliefs; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Nineteenth-century Pacific imperialism; Established: 1 May 1842; Disestablished: 30 December 1880; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Kingdom of Tahuata

Facing regional rivalries and internal warfare, its paramount chief King Iotete concluded an accord with French naval commander Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars in May 1842, placing the island under French protection from his royal seat at Vaitahu. name: Kingdom of Taiohae

Ruled by the local Te Moana dynasty, the kingdom accepted a French protectorate in May 1842 under admiral Du Petit-Thouars, becoming France's principal naval base in the archipelago. Local hereditary rulers retained ceremonial status and limited domestic jurisdiction until the French colonial administration formally abolished the indigenous chieftaincy in July 1901. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Taiohae; Common languages: Marquesan and French; Religion: Traditional Marquesan religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Te Moana; Ruler title: King; Historical era: French Pacific expansion; Established: 1 May 1842; Disestablished: 1 July 1901; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Kingdom of Tahiti

Governed from Papeete, the Tahitian monarchy retained nominal authority over civil matters, but French resident officers seized effective command over external relations, coastal policing and internal security. Widespread local unrest and diplomatic protests from British missionaries led to direct French military annexation in November 1843, touching off the Franco-Tahitian War. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Papeete; Common languages: Tahitian and French; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pomare dynasty; Head of state: Queen Pomare IV; Historical era: Franco-Tahitian conflict; Established: 9 September 1842; Disestablished: 6 November 1843; Succeeded by: Colony of Tahiti

name: Cerrito Government

Headed by former president Manuel Oribe and heavily supported by Argentine confederate forces under Juan Manuel de Rosas, the regime established its seat at Cerrito de la Victoria and built a functioning civil state with judicial tribunals, schools and trade at nearby Villa Restauracion. name: Emirate of Bohtan

description: The Emirate of Bohtan was a powerful autonomous Kurdish principality centred on the fortified island city of Cizre along the upper Tigris River in northern Upper Mesopotamia. Under the energetic leadership of Mir Bedir Khan Beg, the emirate defied Ottoman centralisation policies, minted its own coinage and asserted hegemony across vast tracts of historical Kurdistan. Following bloody intercommunal campaigns against Assyrian Christians and mounting insubordination, imperial Ottoman armies launched a comprehensive military expedition that captured Bedir Khan and annexed the emirate in 1847. \n\n Status: Autonomous principality; Capital: Cizre; Common languages: Kurdish, Arabic and Syriac; Religion: Sunni Islam and Yazidism; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Azizan; Ruler title: Mir; Historical era: Late Ottoman Kurdistan; Established: 1843; Disestablished: 1848; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: French Somaliland

The colony acquired major strategic and commercial importance with the completion of the Franco-Ethiopian railway linking Djibouti's deepwater port to Addis Ababa. name: Mohammadgarh State
description: Mohammadgarh State was a small Muslim princely domain on the fertile Malwa plateau of central India, originally created through a dynastic partition of the neighbouring Kurwai principality. Governed from the town of Mohammadgarh, the realm navigated the shifting balance of regional power between rival Maratha chieftains and British political officers during the mid-nineteenth century. Its ruling nawabs exercised sovereign domestic authority over a compact agricultural territory before formalising subsidiary treaty relations under the Central India Agency in the 1850s. \n\n Status: Autonomous princely state; Capital: Mohammadgarh; Common languages: Urdu, Hindi and Malvi; Religion: Islam and Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Firoz Khel; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Pre-rebellion princely India; Established: 1843; Reorganised: 1851; Succeeded by: Mohammadgarh State (British Raj)

name: Colony of Natal
description: The Colony of Natal was a British Crown colony in south-eastern Africa, established following the military annexation of the short-lived Boer Republic of Natalia in May 1843. Administered from Pietermaritzburg, the colony developed an export-orientated sugar cane economy along its coastal belt, which prompted the large-scale importation of indentured labourers from India alongside the indigenous Zulu population. Natal received responsible parliamentary government in 1893 before joining with neighbouring territories in May 1910 to form the Union of South Africa. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Pietermaritzburg; Common languages: English, Zulu, Dutch and Hindi; Religion: Christianity, Hinduism and Islam; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: British monarch; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: British Southern Africa; Established: 4 May 1843; Disestablished: 31 May 1910; Succeeded by: Union of South Africa

name: Santo Tomás
description: Santo Tomás was a Belgian colonial concession on the Atlantic coast of Guatemala, administered by the Belgian Colonisation Company under a land grant from the Central American government. Headquartered near modern Puerto Barrios, the settlement aimed to establish an agricultural and trading enclave for European immigrants under the sponsorship of King Leopold I. However, widespread tropical illnesses, financial mismanagement and harsh living conditions caused devastating mortality among the colonists, leading to the venture's abandonment by 1855. \n\n Status: Chartered company concession; Administrative seat: Santo Tomas de Castilla; Common languages: French, Dutch and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Commercial chartered administration; Historical era: Nineteenth-century European colonisation; Established: 4 May 1843; Disestablished: 1855; Succeeded by: Republic of Guatemala

name: State of Perlis
description: The State of Perlis was a small Malay sultanate on the north-western coastline of the Malay Peninsula, established when the Siamese kingdom partitioned the realm of Kedah and installed Syed Hussein Jamalullail as its hereditary Raja. Centred at Kangar, the state maintained internal administrative autonomy while dispatching the symbolic bunga mas tribute to the royal court in Bangkok. The ruling Jamalullail dynasty presided over the principality as an independent entity until the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 transferred suzerainty to Great Britain. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate under Siamese suzerainty; Capital: Kangar; Common languages: Kedah Malay and Siamese; Religion: Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jamalullail dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Pre-colonial Malaya; Established: 20 May 1843; Reorganised: 1910; Succeeded by: Unfederated Malay States

name: Amsterdam Island
description: Amsterdam Island was an isolated volcanic possession in the southern Indian Ocean, formally claimed for France in June 1843 by Governor Adam Darmois of Reunion. Uninhabited by any permanent indigenous population, the windswept island served primarily as a navigational landmark for whaling and merchant vessels navigating the Roaring Forties. French authorities established scientific observation huts and later the Martin-de-Vivies research station before integrating the territory into the French Southern and Antarctic Lands in August 1955. \n\n Status: French overseas possession; Administrative seat: None (unsettled island); Official languages: French; Government: Direct naval administration; Historical era: French colonial expansion; Established: 8 June 1843; Disestablished: 6 August 1955; Succeeded by: French Southern and Antarctic Lands

name: Saint-Paul Island
description: Saint-Paul Island was an uninhabited subantarctic volcanic island situated in the southern Indian Ocean roughly ninety kilometres south of Amsterdam Island. Claimed by French naval authorities on 8 June 1843, the rugged terrain featured an open flooded caldera that occasionally sheltered seal hunters, fishermen and scientific expeditions from Reunion. Lacking permanent human habitation, the territory remained under French maritime jurisdiction until its formal incorporation into the overseas territory of the French Southern and Antarctic Lands in 1955. \n\n Status: French overseas possession; Administrative seat: None (uninhabited island); Official languages: French; Government: Direct naval administration; Historical era: French maritime expansion; Established: 8 June 1843; Disestablished: 6 August 1955; Succeeded by: French Southern and Antarctic Lands

name: Kingdom of Sanwi
description: The Kingdom of Sanwi was a traditional Anyi monarchy located in south-eastern Ivory Coast, having been founded around 1740 by Akan migrants from the adjacent Gold Coast region. Centred at its historic royal capital of Krindjabo, the realm entered into a formal treaty of protection with France in September 1843 to safeguard its sovereignty against regional Asante expansionism. Sanwi retained its indigenous royal institutions and ceremonial authority throughout the colonial era before fully merging into the independent Republic of Ivory Coast in 1960. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Krindjabo; Common languages: Anyi and French; Religion: Traditional Akan religion and Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Amon; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial and colonial West Africa; Established: 23 September 1843; Disestablished: 1960; Succeeded by: Republic of Ivory Coast

name: Colony of Tahiti
description: The Colony of Tahiti was a French colonial holding established when French naval officers deposed the indigenous administration and assumed direct military governance over Tahiti and neighbouring Society Islands. Headquartered at Papeete, colonial authorities suppressed widespread resistance from local loyalists during the Franco-Tahitian War before restoring Queen Pomare IV to a purely ceremonial protectorate role. Direct colonial institutions continued to expand until the territory was officially amalgamated into the wider administration of the French Establishments in Oceania in 1903. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Papeete; Common languages: French and Tahitian; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Direct military and civil administration; Ruler title: Governor; Historical era: Nineteenth-century Pacific colonisation; Established: 6 November 1843; Disestablished: 1904; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: !Gami-‡nun
description: !Gami-‡nun was an autonomous Nama community, known historically as the Bondelswarts, established across the arid plains of southern Namibia north of the Orange River. Governed from the settlement of Warmbad by hereditary captains of the Morris and Christian lineages, the polity maintained pastoralist independence through skilled horsemanship and rifle marksmanship. The captains negotiated trade agreements and repelled encroaching rivals until Imperial Germany established colonial authority over South West Africa in August 1890. \n\n Status: Sovereign traditional chieftaincy; Capital: Warmbad; Common languages: Khoekhoe and Dutch; Religion: Traditional Nama beliefs and Christianity; Government: Chieftaincy; Ruler title: Captain; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1844; Disestablished: 21 August 1890; Succeeded by: German South West Africa

name: Antankarana Kingdom
description: The Antankarana Kingdom was a traditional realm situated across the limestone tsingy formations of northernmost Madagascar, having separated from the Sakalava monarchy during seventeenth-century dynastic disputes. Facing intense military incursions from the central highland Merina Kingdom, King Tsimiaro negotiated a treaty of protection with French naval envoys from Reunion in 1844. The kingdom retained domestic autonomy and aided French expeditionary campaigns against the Merina court until France established full colonial dominion over Madagascar in 1896. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Antankarana; Common languages: Malagasy and French; Religion: Traditional Malagasy religion and Islam; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Madagascar; Established: 1844; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: Malagasy Protectorate

name: Basutoland
description: Basutoland was a British Crown colony encompassing the mountainous highlands of modern Lesotho, founded through the diplomacy of King Moshoeshoe I to preserve his Basotho kingdom from Boer encroachment. Administered from Maseru under a British Resident Commissioner, the territory was briefly annexed to the Cape Colony before returning to direct imperial control following the Gun War of 1880. Basutoland maintained its distinct identity and traditional chieftainship structures until achieving complete independence as the Kingdom of Lesotho in October 1966. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Maseru; Common languages: Sesotho and English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: British monarch; Representative title: Resident Commissioner; Currency: Pound sterling; Historical era: British Southern Africa; Established: 1844; Disestablished: 4 October 1966; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Lesotho

name: Kingdom of Tahiti
description: The Kingdom of Tahiti functioned as a French protectorate following the conclusion of the Franco-Tahitian War, which reinstated Queen Pomare IV to the royal throne under close French administrative supervision. Headquartered at Papeete, the kingdom preserved its native code of laws and traditional district chieftaincies while French resident commissioners directed foreign policy, judicial appeals and public finances. The protectorate endured through the reign of King Pomare V until he formally ceded the kingdom to direct French colonial annexation in 1880. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Papeete; Common languages: Tahitian and French; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy under colonial protectorate; Ruling dynasty: Pomare dynasty; Ruler title: Monarch; Currency: French franc; Historical era: French Pacific imperialism; Established: 1844; Disestablished: 1881; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Kingdom of Mangareva
description: The Kingdom of Mangareva was an insular Polynesian monarchy encompassing the volcanic Gambier Islands in south-eastern French Polynesia. Centred at the settlement of Rikitea, the realm was governed by hereditary paramount chiefs titled the akariki, whose authority operated in close coordination with Catholic missionaries of the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. The kingdom accepted French protectorate status in January 1844 and maintained local royal governance until France formally annexed the archipelago in July 1881. \n\n Status: Protectorate of France; Capital: Rikitea; Common languages: Mangarevan and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Te Akariki; Ruler title: Akariki; Historical era: French Pacific expansion; Established: 16 January 1844; Disestablished: 5 July 1881; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Dominican Republic
description: The Dominican Republic gained independence in February 1844 when a nationalist movement led by Juan Pablo Duarte and the Trinitaria society successfully revolted against Haitian occupation on eastern Hispaniola. Governed from the historic capital of Santo Domingo, the First Republic faced constant military threats from Haiti alongside fierce factional struggles between conservative general Pedro Santana and liberal rivals. Crippled by financial bankruptcy and fearing renewed Haitian invasion, Santana orchestrated the republic's voluntary reincorporation into the Spanish Empire in March 1861. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Santo Domingo; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Presidential republic; Head of state: Pedro Santana; Currency: Dominican peso; Historical era: First Dominican Republic; Established: 27 February 1844; Disestablished: 18 March 1861; Preceded by: Republic of Haiti; Succeeded by: Spanish Santo Domingo

name: Republic of Winburg-Potchefstroom
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Winburg-Potchefstroom was a Boer republic formed through the political confederation of Voortrekker communities north of the Orange and Vaal rivers in southern Africa. Governed from Potchefstroom under the leadership of Commandant-General Andries Hendrik Potgieter, the state maintained an elected adjunct Volksraad to regulate land grants and organise mutual defence against hostile indigenous neighbours. The polity was dissolved in February 1848 when the British Crown proclaimed the Orange River Sovereignty over the territory south of the Vaal. \n\n Status: Boer republic; Capital: Potchefstroom; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Federal republic; Head of state: Andries Hendrik Potgieter; Historical era: The Great Trek; Established: 1845; Disestablished: 3 February 1848; Succeeded by: Orange River Sovereignty

name: Basilan
description: Basilan was an ephemeral French colonial outpost established on the strategic island of Basilan in the Sulu Archipelago of the southern Philippines. Seeking a naval coaling station to rival British Singapore, French naval captain Francois Page coerced the Sultan of Sulu into ceding the island and founded a fortified post at Isabela in February 1845. However, strenuous diplomatic protests from the Spanish Empire regarding historic sovereignty and the refusal of King Louis-Philippe to ratify the treaty led French forces to evacuate the island that August. \n\n Status: French colonial possession; Capital: Isabela; Common languages: French, Yakan, Tausug and Spanish; Religion: Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Naval military administration; Ruler title: French monarch; Historical era: Nineteenth-century European colonial rivalry; Established: 20 February 1845; Disestablished: 5 August 1845; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Sulu

name: Habr Yunis Sultanate
description: The Habr Yunis Sultanate was an influential Somali monarchy that governed extensive pasturelands and inland caravan routes across the Horn of Africa, within present-day Somaliland and eastern Ethiopia. Centred at Burao and ruled by the hereditary Rer Ainanshe lineage of the Isaaq clan family, the sultanate commanded formidable cavalry formations to regulate regional livestock trade with the Red Sea port of Berbera. The sultanate maintained political independence throughout the nineteenth century before fracturing under internal succession disputes and British colonial protectorate consolidation by 1908. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Burao; Common languages: Somali and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Rer Ainanshe; Ruler title: Suldaan; Historical era: Precolonial Horn of Africa; Established: 1846; Disestablished: 1908; Succeeded by: British Somaliland

name: Kingdom of Cambodia
description: The Kingdom of Cambodia functioned as a shared condominium under joint Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty following decades of devastating warfare between the two rival regional empires. Governed by King Ang Duong from the royal capital of Oudong and later Phnom Penh, the Khmer court had to pay tribute simultaneously to Bangkok and Hue while striving to preserve national culture and territorial integrity. To escape this crushing dual subjugation, King Norodom signed a treaty with French naval officers in August 1863, transforming Cambodia into a French protectorate. \n\n Status: Condominium under Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty; Capital: Phnom Penh; Common languages: Khmer, Siamese and Vietnamese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 1846; Disestablished: 11 August 1863; Succeeded by: French Protectorate of Cambodia

name: Masubia
description: Masubia was an autonomous Bantu kingdom established across the lush floodplains of the Zambezi and Chobe rivers in the eastern Caprivi region. Governed by hereditary monarchs known as the Liswani from their royal headquarters at Bukalo, the realm developed a cattle-rearing and fishing economy adapted to seasonal inundations. The kingdom preserved its cultural integrity and internal sovereignty against regional Lozi and Kololo hegemony until falling under British colonial influence in March 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign traditional kingdom; Capital: Bukalo; Common languages: Subia and Lozi; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Precolonial Southern Africa; Established: 1846; Disestablished: 23 March 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Nalu
description: The Nalu kingdom was a sovereign coastal polity established along the lower Rio Nunez and surrounding estuaries in maritime Guinea. Centred at Kassou, the realm was governed by indigenous lineages whose sociopolitical authority was reinforced through the sacred Simo initiation society. The kingdom maintained lucrative trade relations with European merchants while fiercely defending its agrarian hinterland until French colonial forces subjugated the region in 1892. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kassou; Common languages: Nalu; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial West Africa; Established: 1846; Disestablished: 1892; Succeeded by: French Guinea

name: Suket State
label: indian princely states
description: Suket State was a prominent Himalayan princely domain located in the rugged valleys of the Punjab Hills in modern Himachal Pradesh. Founded by ancient Rajput lineages and governed from its administrative seat at Mandi and later Sundernagar, the state entered into subsidiary alliance with the British East India Company in 1846 following the First Anglo-Sikh War. The ruling dynasty maintained domestic civil jurisdiction under the Punjab Hill States Agency until formally acceding to independent India in April 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Mandi; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely state; Ruling dynasty: Suket Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1846; Disestablished: 15 April 1948; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Colony of North Australia
label: british colonies in australia
description: The Colony of North Australia was a short-lived British colonial administrative project authorised by letters patent in February 1846 to establish a separate dependency in northern Queensland. Intended primarily as a pastoral settlement and penal colony for conditionally pardoned convicts, the administration was projected to operate from Port Curtis near modern Gladstone under Superintendent George Barney. However, a change of government in London led to the prompt revocation of the colonial charter in December 1847 before permanent civil institutions could be consolidated. \n\n Status: British Crown colony; Capital: Gladstone; Common languages: English; Religion: Christianity; Government: Colonial administration; Ruler title: British monarch; Representative title: Superintendent; Historical era: Victorian era; Established: 17 February 1846; Disestablished: 28 December 1847; Succeeded by: Colony of New South Wales

name: Mexican Republic (Military Occupation)
description: The Mexican Republic (Military Occupation) designates the contested border zone between the Rio Grande and the Nueces River occupied by Mexican forces under General Mariano Arista in the spring of 1846. Operating from mobile military encampments opposite Fort Texas, Arista crossed the Rio Grande to challenge American troop deployments in territory claimed by both nations. Following fierce clashes at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma, Mexican units were forced to retreat across the river in May 1846, marking the formal onset of the Mexican-American War. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile military encampment; Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military command; Ruler title: General; Historical era: Mexican-American War; Established: 25 April 1846; Disestablished: 9 May 1846; Succeeded by: United States Army

name: California Republic
description: The California Republic was a short-lived insurgent state proclaimed at Sonoma in June 1846 by American settlers rebelling against Mexican departmental governance. Known colloquially as the Bear Flag Republic, the movement was headed by William B. Ide and encouraged covertly by United States Army officer John C. Fremont. The fledgling administration exercised military control north of San Francisco Bay for several weeks before dissolving itself when regular American naval forces landed and claimed California for the United States. \n\n Status: Unrecognised breakaway republic; Capital: Sonoma; Common languages: English and Spanish; Religion: Protestantism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary republic; Head of state: William B. Ide; Historical era: Mexican-American War; Established: 14 June 1846; Disestablished: 9 July 1846; Succeeded by: United States military government of California

name: United Mexican States
description: The United Mexican States restored constitutional federalism in August 1846 when interim president Jose Mariano Salas reinstated the liberal Constitution of 1824, inaugurating the Second Federal Republic. Governed from Mexico City, the revitalised federation was immediately plunged into the disastrous Mexican-American War, which resulted in the loss of upper California and New Mexico under the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The state subsequently weathered the bitter Reform War and sustained French military intervention before liberal forces under Benito Juarez achieved final victory in June 1867. \n\n Status: Sovereign federal republic; Capital: Ciudad de Mexico; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal presidential republic; Ruler title: President; Currency: Mexican real; Historical era: Second Federal Republic of Mexico; Established: 22 August 1846; Disestablished: 19 June 1867; Succeeded by: Second Mexican Empire

name: Chamba State
label: indian princely states
description: Chamba State was an ancient Hindu hill principality nestled in the upper Ravi River basin of the Western Himalayas, having preserved its autonomy since the sixth century. Administered from its picturesque valley capital at Chamba, the state came under British imperial suzerainty in September 1846 following the defeat of the Sikh Empire. The ruling Rajput dynasty maintained progressive domestic governance and forestry management under the Punjab States Agency until the final ruler acceded to the Indian Union in April 1948. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Chamba; Common languages: Chambeali and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Varman; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 3 September 1846; Disestablished: 1949; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: British Concession in Shanghai
label: concessions in china
description: The British Concession in Shanghai was a privileged foreign commercial enclave established along the western bank of the Huangpu River following the First Opium War. Administered from its municipal council offices in Shanghai under British consular oversight, the settlement possessed its own police force, tax authority and extraterritorial judicial protections. In September 1863, the British concession amalgamated with the neighbouring American enclave to form the Shanghai International Settlement. \n\n Status: Foreign municipal concession; Administrative seat: Shanghai; Common languages: English and Chinese; Religion: Anglicanism and Protestantism; Government: Municipal council under consular oversight; Historical era: Treaty port era; Established: 20 November 1846; Disestablished: 21 September 1863; Succeeded by: Shanghai International Settlement

name: Crown Colony of Labuan
description: The Crown Colony of Labuan began as a strategic naval coaling depot off the north-western coast of Borneo, ceded to Great Britain by the Sultan of Brunei in December 1846. Governed from the harbour settlement of Victoria, British naval commanders initially administered the island to suppress regional piracy and secure shipping lanes connecting Singapore and Hong Kong. This transitional military administration was converted into a formal civil Crown colony in August 1848 under the governorship of James Brooke. \n\n Status: British Crown dependency; Capital: Victoria; Common languages: English and Malay; Religion: Christianity and Islam; Government: Naval colonial administration; Ruler title: British monarch; Historical era: British Empire; Established: 18 December 1846; Reorganised: 1 August 1848; Succeeded by: Crown Colony of Labuan

name: Jammu and Kashmir
label: indian princely states
description: Jammu and Kashmir was a sprawling princely state created in the Western Himalayas after Maharaja Gulab Singh acquired the Kashmir Valley from the British under the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar. Administered between the dual capitals of Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer, the realm united diverse alpine regions including Ladakh, Gilgit and Baltistan under Dogra Rajput governance. As the paramount princely state of northern British India, it maintained extensive internal autonomy until contested accession to the Dominion of India in 1947 precipitated the First Indo-Pakistani War. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Srinagar; Common languages: Kashmiri, Dogri, Urdu and Punjabi; Religion: Islam, Hinduism and Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Hereditary absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jamwal Dogra; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1847; Disestablished: 15 August 1947; Succeeded by: Dominion of India

name: Kapurthala State
label: indian princely states
description: Kapurthala State was a prominent Sikh princely realm situated in the fertile Doaba region between the Beas and Sutlej rivers in the Punjab. Governed from its historic capital at Kapurthala by the Ahluwalia dynasty, the state accepted British suzerainty following the First Anglo-Sikh War while preserving domestic administrative sovereignty. The ruling maharajas gained renown for progressive educational initiatives and cultural patronages, maintaining communal harmony across Sikh, Muslim and Hindu populations until acceding to the Indian Union in 1947. \n\n Status: Princely state under British suzerainty; Capital: Kapurthala; Common languages: Punjabi and Urdu; Religion: Sikhism, Islam and Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ahluwalia; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: British Raj; Established: 1847; Disestablished: 1948; Succeeded by: Patiala and East Punjab States Union

name: Republic of Klip River
label: boer states
description: The Republic of Klip River was an ephemeral Boer polity established by Voortrekkers under the leadership of Andries Spies in northern Natal. Occupying fertile grazing lands between the Tugela and Buffalo rivers with its main centre near modern Ladysmith, the community acquired territorial rights through negotiations with Zulu monarch Mpande. The breakaway republic sought complete independence from British coastal jurisdiction, but was forcibly annexed to the Colony of Natal by Cape Governor Sir Harry Smith in early 1848. \n\n Status: Unrecognised Boer republic; Administrative seat: Ladysmith; Common languages: Dutch and Afrikaans; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church; Government: Republic; Head of state: Andries Spies; Historical era: The Great Trek; Established: 1847; Disestablished: 1848; Succeeded by: Colony of Natal

name: Taos Rebels
description: The Taos Rebels were an insurgent alliance of northern New Mexican Hispano and Puebloan fighters who launched a sudden rebellion against United States military occupation during the Mexican-American War. Operating from fortified positions at Taos Pueblo under the leadership of Pablo Montoya and Tomas Romero, the insurgents killed the newly appointed American governor Charles Bent. United States military forces under Colonel Sterling Price swiftly converged on Taos and stormed the fortified adobe church in February 1847, brutally suppressing the uprising. \n\n Status: Insurgent revolutionary alliance; Administrative seat: Taos Pueblo; Common languages: Spanish and Tiwa; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Pueblo religion; Government: Insurgent council; Historical era: Mexican-American War; Established: 3 February 1847; Disestablished: 5 February 1847; Succeeded by: United States provisional government of New Mexico

name: Republic of Guatemala
description: The Republic of Guatemala was formally established as a sovereign nation in March 1847 when President Rafael Carrera severed all remaining ties to the moribund Federal Republic of Central America. Governed from Guatemala City, the Carrera regime pursued conservative domestic policies, restored institutional privileges to the Catholic Church and expanded agrarian production. The republic defended its national borders against liberal filibusters and neighbouring regional powers throughout the nineteenth century, developing into a major coffee exporter. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital and largest city: Guatemala City; Official languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Rafael Carrera; Currency: Guatemalan peso; Historical era: Nineteenth-century Central America; Established: 21 March 1847; Legislature: Congress of the Republic

name: Republic of Liberia
description: The Republic of Liberia was established on the Atlantic coastline of West Africa as an independent sovereign state proclaimed by freed Black emigrants from North America in July 1847. Governed from the port city of Monrovia, the young commonwealth drafted a republican constitution modelled on that of the United States and elected Joseph Jenkins Roberts as its first president. The Americo-Liberian leadership maintained national sovereignty throughout the European Scramble for Africa while gradually expanding administrative authority over indigenous interior populations. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Monrovia; Official languages: English; Common languages: English, Kpelle and Bassa; Religion: Protestant Christianity; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Joseph Jenkins Roberts; Ruler title: President; Currency: Liberian dollar; Historical era: Nineteenth-century West Africa; Established: 16 July 1847; Legislature: Legislature of Liberia

name: Chan Santa Cruz
description: Chan Santa Cruz was an autonomous Maya theocratic state founded in the dense tropical forests of the eastern Yucatan Peninsula during the fierce Caste War against Hispanic rule. Centred on the holy sanctuary of Noj Kaaj Santa Cruz Xbaalam Naj, the polity was united by the Cruzoob faith, which venerated the sacred Talking Cross that issued divine military directives. Sustained by British trade through neighbouring Belize, the Maya state resisted Mexican federal incursions for decades before its capital was occupied by federal forces in 1901. \n\n Status: Autonomous indigenous state; Capital: Chan Santa Cruz; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Cruzoob religion; Government: Theocratic chiefdom; Ruler title: Halach Uinik; Historical era: Caste War of Yucatan; Established: 26 August 1847; Disestablished: 1936; Preceded by: Republic of Yucatan; Succeeded by: United Mexican States

name: Kingdom of Bora Bora
description: The Kingdom of Bora Bora was an independent Polynesian island state encompassing Bora Bora alongside the neighbouring atolls of Maupiti, Tupai and Maupihaa in the Leeward Society Islands. Governed from Vaitape by monarchs of the Tapoa dynasty, the realm attained international recognition through the Anglo-French Jarnac Convention of 1847. The kingdom maintained traditional laws, Protestant ecclesiastical schools and domestic autonomy until the French colonial administration deposed Queen Teriimaevarua III and completed formal annexation in 1895. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Vaitape; Common languages: Tahitian and French; Religion: Protestant Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Tapoa; Ruler title: Monarch; Currency: French franc; Historical era: Precolonial Oceania; Established: 1848; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: French Establishments in Oceania

name: Orange River Sovereignty
description: The Orange River Sovereignty was a British Crown dependency proclaimed by Cape Colony Governor Sir Harry Smith over the vast plateau between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Administered from Bloemfontein by a British Resident, the authority sought to maintain peace among rival Boer farmers, Griqua captains and King Moshoeshoe's Basotho people. Faced with persistent frontier skirmishes and unwilling to bear the financial burden of interior garrisons, the British government signed the Bloemfontein Convention in February 1854, relinquishing authority to the newly independent Orange Free State. \n\n Status: British Crown dependency; Capital: Bloemfontein; Common languages: Dutch, English and Sesotho; Religion: Dutch Reformed Church and Christianity; Government: Crown administration; Representative title: British Resident; Historical era: Victorian era; Established: 3 February 1848; Disestablished: 23 February 1854; Succeeded by: Orange Free State

name: French Republic
description: The French Republic, commonly referred to as the Second Republic, was inaugurated in February 1848 following the popular revolution that toppled King Louis-Philippe and the July Monarchy. Governed from Paris, the provisional administration introduced universal male suffrage, abolished slavery across French colonial territories and enacted democratic labour reforms. Plagued by ideological strife between moderate republicans and socialist factions, the republic came to an end after President Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte orchestrated an authoritarian coup d'etat in December 1851 and restored the French Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Paris; Official languages: French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unitary presidential republic; Head of state: Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte; Currency: French franc; Historical era: Revolutions of 1848; Established: 25 February 1848; Disestablished: 2 December 1852; Succeeded by: Second French Empire

name: Provisional Government of Milan
description: The Provisional Government of Milan was a revolutionary regime established in March 1848 during the celebrated Five Days insurrection that expelled Austrian imperial troops under Field Marshal Radetzky from Lombardy. Led by Count Gabrio Casati from municipal headquarters in Milan, the moderate aristocratic council coordinated urban defence and requested military assistance from King Charles Albert of Sardinia. The provisional authority promoted the fusion of Lombardy with Piedmont before the defeat of Sardinian forces at Custoza permitted Austrian armies to reoccupy the city in August 1848. \n\n Status: Revolutionary provisional government; Capital: Milan; Common languages: Italian and Lombard; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Provisional municipal junta; Head of state: Gabrio Casati; Historical era: First Italian War of Independence; Established: 18 March 1848; Disestablished: 8 June 1848; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia

name: Free Cities of Mentone and Roccabruna
description: The Free Cities of Mentone and Roccabruna were an autonomous municipal federation formed along the Riviera coast when the populations of Menton and Roquebrune revolted against the extractive rule of Prince Florestan I of Monaco. Governed from Mentone by an elected provisional committee, the cities declared themselves independent communes and placed their territory under the royal protection of the Kingdom of Sardinia. The two free towns maintained self-governing status until Sardinia was officially forced to reorganise border zones and later transfer the territory to France in 1860. \n\n Status: Autonomous urban federation; Capital: Mentone; Common languages: Mentonasque, French and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal federation; Historical era: Revolutions of 1848; Established: 21 March 1848; Disestablished: 1 May 1849; Preceded by: Principality of Monaco; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia

name: Republic of San Marco
description: The Republic of San Marco was an Italian revolutionary state proclaimed in the Venetian Lagoon in March 1848 after citizens rose in revolt and expelled the Austrian military garrison. Led by Daniele Manin from the historic capital of Venice, the republic re-established self-rule across the Venetian terraferma and joined in common cause with the Kingdom of Sardinia against Habsburg domination. The maritime state endured a protracted Austrian naval blockade and bombardment before disease, starvation and relentless shelling forced its heroic surrender in August 1849. \n\n Status: Revolutionary republic; Capital: Venice; Common languages: Venetian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Republic; Head of state: Daniele Manin; Ruler title: President; Currency: Venetian lira; Historical era: Revolutions of 1848; Established: 22 March 1848; Disestablished: 24 August 1849; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia

name: Duchies of Schleswig-Holstein
description: The Duchies of Schleswig-Holstein designates the revolutionary provisional government established at Kiel in March 1848 by German nationalists rejecting the authority of the Danish Crown. Backed by the Frankfurt National Assembly and Prussian military units, the insurgent regime sought to unite Schleswig and Holstein as an autonomous member state of the German Confederation. The government prosecuted the First Schleswig War against Denmark until international diplomatic pressure from the Great Powers forced Prussian withdrawal and the restoration of Danish royal suzerainty in April 1851. \n\n Status: Provisional revolutionary government; Administrative seat: Kiel; Common languages: German and Danish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Provisional directory; Historical era: First Schleswig War; Established: 24 March 1848; Disestablished: 1 April 1851; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Denmark

name: Kingdom of Sicily
description: The Kingdom of Sicily was an independent constitutional monarchy revived in March 1848 during a widespread insurrection against the Bourbon dynasty of the Two Sicilies. Centred at Palermo, the revolutionary parliament restored the liberal Sicilian Constitution of 1812 and deposed King Ferdinand II, offering the island's crown to Prince Ferdinand of Savoy. However, Bourbon expeditionary forces commanded by General Carlo Filangieri launched a brutal military campaign that recaptured the island and restored Neapolitan royal control in May 1849. \n\n Status: Revolutionary constitutional kingdom; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Constitutional monarchy; Ruler title: King; Legislature: Parliament of Sicily; Currency: Sicilian piastra; Historical era: Sicilian Revolution of 1848; Established: 25 March 1848; Disestablished: 15 May 1849; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

name: Kingdom of Sardinia (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Sardinia (Military Occupation) denotes the operational military administration exercised by the Royal Sardinian Army over liberated territories in northern and central Italy during the First and Second Wars of Italian Independence. Directed from mobile military headquarters under King Charles Albert and later King Victor Emmanuel II, these field zones temporarily governed cities and supply lines across Lombardy and the central duchies. The occupation structures coordinated local militia forces and plebiscites until formal political annexation into the emergent Kingdom of Italy was completed. \n\n Status: Military occupation zone; Administrative seat: Mobile military headquarters; Common languages: Italian, Piedmontese and French; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administration; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Italian Risorgimento; Established: 29 March 1848; Disestablished: 17 March 1861; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Chan Santa Cruz
description: Chan Santa Cruz in this wider insurgent context represents the decentralised network of autonomous Maya rebel communities that waged the Caste War across the dense jungles of the Yucatan Peninsula. Operating from shifting forest encampments and hidden settlements without a single fixed capital city, Maya warlords directed guerrilla operations against Yucatecan and Mexican federal troops. Driven by indigenous cultural resilience and religious devotion, the fighters retained control over eastern Yucatan until federal armies under General Ignacio Bravo completed the pacification campaign in May 1901. \n\n Status: Autonomous indigenous confederacy; Administrative seat: Shifting rebel encampments; Common languages: Yucatec Maya; Religion: Cruzoob religion; Government: Decentralised military council; Ruler title: Supreme general; Historical era: Caste War of Yucatan; Established: 1 June 1848; Disestablished: 5 May 1901; Succeeded by: United Mexican States

name: Austria-Hungary (Military Occupation)
description: Austria-Hungary (Military Occupation) refers to the transitional imperial military administration established by the Austrian army over rebellious and conquered territories across northern Italy and the Adriatic littoral during the 1848-1849 uprisings and subsequent conflicts. Commanded by imperial field marshals such as Joseph Radetzky without an independent civil capital, the administration enforced martial law, suppressed revolutionary committees and requisitioned civilian resources. These temporary commands persisted until civic Habsburg governance could be re-established or territories transferred by international treaty. \n\n Status: Imperial military occupation; Administrative seat: Field headquarters; Common languages: German, Italian and Hungarian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: Field Marshal; Historical era: Mid-nineteenth-century European revolutions; Established: 25 July 1848; Disestablished: 10 September 1919; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Italy

name: Crown Colony of Labuan
